In Daniel 2:28-29, the secret of Nebuchadnezzar—what will happen in the future—can only be understood by the God of heaven, who "reveals secrets." It is the idea that certain essential truths surpass human wisdom and require divine revelation. 3. The secret can also be a thought or intention of the heart, as in Daniel 2:30: "the thoughts of your heart" are a secret that the king carried within himself without saying, and that only God could know.
H7328.origine: This Hebrew word raz means originally "what is hidden, what must remain closed." It is borrowed from neighboring ancient Semitic languages and reveals the idea that certain realities cannot be grasped by simple observation or reason. In the Old Testament, the word appears mainly in the book of Daniel, which deals with visions and divine revelations: it is a word suited to the context of celestial mysteries and the hidden intentions of God.
H7328.emploi: This word appears 8 times in Hebrew, only in the book of Daniel (chapters 2 and 4), a book that speaks of prophetic dreams and divine revelations. In the account of chapter 2, Nebuchadnezzar asks the wise men to reveal his dream, but only God, through Daniel, can do so: the king's secret becomes a sign of God's power. The word is also used for God's ability to know and reveal ("the one who reveals secrets"), showing that nothing escapes the divine gaze. In Daniel 2:47, the king acknowledges that the God of Daniel is "the God of gods and the Lord of kings, and the one who reveals secrets": the secret becomes the living proof of God's sovereignty.
H7328.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that God is not limited by our ignorance: he knows what escapes us, he sees our most hidden thoughts and possesses wisdom that surpasses all human understanding. It is a source of confidence: even when we do not understand God's plans or the future, he alone is the master of it. It also invites humility before the mysteries of his will.

sens: to become thin or emaciated
to lose strength, vigor
to diminish, to gradually disappear
H7329.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to become thin, to lose flesh and bodily substance. In Isaiah 17:4, it is the "fat of Jacob's flesh" that will "vanish" — the image of emaciation, of the body's decline.
2. From this derives the meaning of losing strength, power, or glory. Jacob will see his "glory" weakened as his physical substance diminishes: it is a total decline.
3. The word finally expands to mean "to annihilate" or make disappear: in Zephaniah 2:11, the Lord will "annihilate" all the gods of the earth — not reducing them to nothing in an instant, but weakening them, stripping them of their power until they are brought to nothing.
H7329.origine: The Hebrew root רזה (razah) expresses the idea of thinness and decline. It comes from a very concrete image: that of a creature or thing that gradually loses its substance, its vital energy. The word belongs to the semantic field of weakening and reduction, which can be physical (the body grows thin) or moral and spiritual (power fades).
H7329.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, in two contexts of divine judgment. In Isaiah 17:4, it describes Jacob's weakening during judgment: his glory and substance vanish together, an image of a once-prosperous nation reduced to misery. In Zephaniah 2:11, the same verb takes on a broader and stronger meaning: the Lord will "annihilate" the gods of the nations, stripping them of all power and worship. In both cases, the word emphasizes a gradual reduction and disappearance of strength or influence.
H7329.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the fragility of human and earthly things — whether national prosperity, personal glory, or even false gods. Before God, everything that turns away from Him weakens and ultimately disappears. It is a call not to place trust in powers that can only decay, but in the Lord alone, whose power is eternal and unshakeable.

sens: Lacking flesh, very slender
Lacking fertility, wealth (for land)
Lacking substance, abundance
H7330.detail:
1. The word first describes a body or animal devoid of fat and flesh: something or someone who has become thin or who does not have enough to eat. It is the opposite image of "fat" — the thin sheep in Ezekiel 34:20 contrasts with the fat sheep, the one that has been well-fed.
2. When speaking of land, the word designates poor, barren soil that produces nothing or very little: when the spies explore Canaan in Numbers 13:20, they must check whether the land is "fat" (rich, fertile) or "thin" (depleted, unproductive). Egypt provides the opposite example: its fat lands swell after the flooding of the Nile.
3. Figuratively, it evokes what lacks substance, value, strength — what does not truly nourish.
H7330.origine: The Hebrew root רָזֶה comes from a family of words expressing thinness and lack of substance. The word paints the visual image of a creature that has lost its fat reserves, either due to lack of food, old age, or illness. The same root is used to describe gradual emaciation.
H7330.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Numbers 13:20, Moses' spies are instructed to observe the promised land and note whether it is fertile (fat) or barren (thin) — it is a practical inquiry into resources. In Ezekiel 34:20, the Lord denounces the shepherds of Israel who have fed themselves while the flock grew weak: He will then establish His judgment between the fat sheep (those favored by the wicked shepherds) and the thin sheep (those who have suffered). The contrast is moral and social.
H7330.portee: This word reminds us that God sees those who suffer from lack — the hungry, the impoverished, the forgotten — and that He does not abandon them. It invites the reader to recognize the difference between those who have abundance and those who lack, and to consider where they stand in their own judgment of the weak.

sens: Syrian adversary of King Solomon
Leader who established a kingdom in Damascus
H7331.detail: Rezon is a man from Syria mentioned only once in the Old Testament. He is the son of Eliada, who fled from his master Hadadezer, king of Zobah, and gathered around him a band of fighters to become a rival king in Syria (1 Kings 11:23). The Bible presents him as one of the enemies that God raised against Solomon at the end of his reign, marking the beginning of troubles that would weaken the united kingdom of Israel.
H7331.origine: The name Rezon means "prince" in Hebrew, which corresponds well to his historical status: a military leader who became the ruler of a small principality.
H7331.emploi: Rezon appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Kings 11:23. He is presented in the context of the adversaries that God raised against Solomon to humiliate his reign. A man of initiative and resources, he took advantage of the political weakening of Northern Syria to establish his own state in Damascus and become a threat to Israel.

sens: State of emaciation, thinness of the body
Disease or physical suffering that gnaws and weakens
Insufficiency, lack or reduced measure
H7332.detail:
1. Decline is primarily the emaciation of the body, when the flesh becomes thin and the strength fades. It is the image of a person who visibly loses weight, deprived of food or consumed by illness. In Isaiah 10:16, God sends decline among the mighty warriors of the king of Assyria, reducing them from within.
2. Decline can also refer to the disease itself, this suffering that progressively consumes. In Psalms 106:15, after the people of Israel eagerly asked for meat, God answered their prayer but "sent decline into their bodies" — a punishment that weakens them through illness.
3. Figuratively, it also refers to lack or insufficiency: a measure that is too small, a reduced or deficient quantity. In Micah 6:10, the prophet denounces the "too small ephah," that is, a dishonest unit of measure, reduced to cheat the poor.
H7332.origine: The Hebrew word razon comes from a root that expresses the idea of thinness and reduction. Its primary image is that of a body that diminishes, becoming thin and weak. This notion extends to anything that lacks, anything that is incomplete or insufficient.
H7332.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Psalms 106:15, it refers to the physical punishment that strikes the overly greedy Israelites. In Isaiah 10:16, God sends it against the Assyrian warriors as a sign of His dominion. In Micah 6:10, it takes on a more concrete meaning: the insufficient, dishonest measure that reduces the weight or quantity sold. In all three cases, it is a negative reality, either a disease or a fraud.
H7332.portee: Decline in the Bible reminds us that hunger, disease, and fraud are real evils that affect the body and material life. For Israel, it is also a sign of divine judgment: God can weaken those who refuse to listen, and He sees dishonesty in commerce and the dishonest scales of the merchant. This word invites the believer to recognize God's hand in the realities of the body and daily life.

sens: Chief of State, sovereign, monarch
H7333.detail: 1. The word designates a political leader or a sovereign who exercises authority over a people. In Proverbs 14:28, it is used in parallel with the king: "When the people are numerous, it is the glory of a king; when the people are lacking, it is the ruin of the prince." The text shows that the prince, like the king, depends on his people — a prince without subjects is a ruined prince; his power and glory rest on the significance of those he governs.
H7333.origine: The Hebrew word razon comes from a root that means "to dominate" or "to reign." It is related to the verb that expresses the exercise of royal power. This term thus designates one who dominates, commands, and imposes his authority.
H7333.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 14:28. It is used in parallel with "king" to describe a political leader. The wisdom context of Proverbs uses it to teach a truth: the strength of a prince or a king lies in the multitude of his people, not in his crown. Without people, the prince is nothing.
H7333.portee: This verse reminds the reader that all earthly power is relative and depends on human factors. It invites those who govern not to despise their people, and those who obey to understand that the people do not exist for the prince, but that the prince exists for the people. It is a lesson in humility for the powerful.

sens: State of a person or body that has lost a lot of weight, who is skeletal
Loss of substance, wasting of the body
Figuratively: loss of self, annihilation of oneself
H7334.detail:
1. The word literally designates the extreme thinness of a body, the visible emaciation of a person. It is the opposite of one who is nourished and vigorous. In Isaiah 24:16, the prophet cries, "I am lost!", expressing his physical and moral wasting in the chaos of divine judgment.
2. The term also suggests the process of wasting away: a body that wears out, that empties of its substance due to famine, illness, or exhaustion. It is a gradual weakening.
3. On a figurative or spiritual level, thinness becomes the image of loss of self, of the nothingness into which one sinks. The prophet uses this word to express his inner annihilation in the face of the calamities that befall the world.
H7334.origine: The Hebrew word רָזִי (razi) likely comes from a root meaning "thin" or "exhausted." It expresses the concrete idea of a person emptied of strength and weight. The root belongs to the family of terms describing physical thinness, the absence of flesh and substance.
H7334.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 24:16. The prophet uses it to express his own state of distress and wasting amid the chaos of divine judgment on the earth. It is a personal and visceral cry: the prophet, witnessing the calamities of the world, feels himself fading away, losing himself, disappearing. The uniqueness of this usage makes the word all the more striking: it concentrates the suffering and annihilation of the prophet into a single image, that of a body that is exhausting and consuming itself.
H7334.portee: This word reminds us that suffering, loss, and wasting are realities that even the prophet experiences. He does not speak from a lofty tower, but from the very heart of distress. For the Christian reader, it illustrates how sin and divine judgment affect not only the body but also the soul of the righteous, who may feel annihilated. It is an invitation to recognize that in the face of the mysteries of evil and judgment, even sincere faith can cry out in distress.

sens: Blinking or flash of the eyes
Gesture of defiance or provocation through the gaze
H7335.detail:
1. The word literally describes a rapid movement of the eyes: either a blink, or a glimmer or a kind of flash of the gaze. It is the basic physical idea.
2. In Job 15:12, Eliphaz uses this word to reproach Job for his "rolling" of the eyes — a gesture that expresses rebellion, defiance, or contempt toward the speaker. The movement of the eyes becomes the visible sign of an inner attitude: pride or protest.
H7335.origine: The root razam paints the image of a flash, a bright light — the idea of something that bursts forth or shines suddenly. It is rare in biblical Hebrew, and it is precisely this image of light that explains the connection with the blinking or glimmering of the eyes, both phenomena involving a quick play of light and shadow.
H7335.emploi: The word appears only once in Job 15:12. Eliphaz, Job's friend, criticizes his attitude: he reproaches him for having a heart carried away by passion and, as a sign of this inner revolt, this "rolling" of the eyes — a gesture of insolence or defiance. In this context, the word denotes less an involuntary movement than a deliberate expression of contempt or rebellion.
H7335.portee: This word reminds us that our gaze speaks as much as our mouth. The eyes reflect what is happening in the heart, and sometimes the silent challenge of a simple look can hurt or insult more than a word. For the believer, it is a call to keep not only our words but also our looks and expressions in accordance with the fear of God.

sens: Political or military leader who exercises power with authority
One who commands, who orders with weight and judgment
One who reigns or governs
H7336.detail:
1. A prince is a leader who holds a commanding authority: in Judges 5:3, the singer addresses the "kings" and "princes" as those who listen and exercise power — these are the figures of authority that the people recognize.
2. The prince is one who "commands what is just" (Proverbs 8:15): it is not just a title, but a function of judgment and governance based on the weight of discernment. A prince who drinks wine loses this ability to judge rightly (Proverbs 31:4).
3. By extension, the word designates anyone who exercises a commanding authority, even if it is rendered null by a superior power (Isaiah 40:23: God reduces princes to nothing).
H7336.origine: The Hebrew word רָזַן (razan) comes from a root that evokes what is heavy, weighty, serious. A prince is one whose word carries weight, whose judgment counts and weighs in the affairs of the people. The same root produces the name רָזֹן (razon), "prince" in the sense of one who governs by the weight of his authority and judgment.
H7336.emploi: This word appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the plural or in a governmental context. It designates political and military leaders, often alongside kings (Judges 5:3; Psalms 2:2). The context shows that princes are responsible for just order (Proverbs 8:15), held to temperance (Proverbs 31:4), and ultimately subject to the sovereignty of God (Isaiah 40:23; Habakkuk 1:10). The word emphasizes less hereditary rank than the exercise of commanding power and judgment.
H7336.portee: This word reminds the reader that true power resides in the ability to judge with justice and wisdom, not in brute force. It also highlights that every prince, every ruler, remains under the supreme authority of God, who can reduce to nothing the most powerful earthly authorities. It is an invitation to respect authority without absolutizing it.

sens: To become wide or spacious, referring to a physical space
To increase in extent or magnitude
To give space, freedom to someone
To prosper or succeed (figuratively)
H7337.detail:
1. The primary meaning is spatial: a place becomes wide, vast, or spacious. In Genesis 26:22, Isaac names a well "Rehoboth" (which means "wide spaces") because "the Lord has now made room for us" — the well represents a space to prosper without conflict, a haven of ease.

2. The word also describes the increase of a reality: anxieties can grow or increase (Psalms 25:17), as if they take up more space in the heart.

3. To extend something to someone is to do good for them and give them an advantage: a gift "enlarges the way" for the one who receives it, meaning it opens doors for them among the great (Proverbs 18:16). In Isaiah 54:2, we are called to enlarge our tent — an image of a house growing to accommodate more people.

4. In a figurative or spiritual sense, "to enlarge" means to prosper, succeed, or be freed. The mouth opens wide when joy overflows or when one triumphs over enemies (1 Samuel 2:1).
H7337.origine: The Hebrew root רחב (ra-chav) expresses the fundamental idea of width and spatial extension. It gives rise to several words: rachav ("wide"), rechav ("chariot," which can be wide), and place names like Rehoboth. The image is one of space opening up, freedom of movement, ease — everything that opposes narrowness and constraint.
H7337.emploi: The verb appears 25 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Psalms, Isaiah, and the wisdom books. It can refer to physical enlargement: a house, a tent, rooms, a well that provides space (Genesis 26:22, Ezekiel 41:7). It can also describe the widening of capacities or opportunities: God enlarges the way of the righteous (Psalms 18:37), gifts enlarge access to the powerful (Proverbs 18:16). Sometimes it translates an abstract increase: anxieties grow, or prosperity increases. The context determines whether it is positive (liberation, success) or neutral (simple enlargement).
H7337.portee: This word reminds us that divine blessing often manifests through space and freedom: God puts us "in a wide place," bringing us out of narrowness. For the believer, it is an invitation to recognize that true prosperity does not come from accumulation, but from freedom of movement and the ability to grow unhindered. It is also a call to share this ease: to enlarge one's tent for others, as Isaiah says.

sens: The extent of a space in its horizontal dimension
An open, vast space, without obstacles
Freedom, absence of constraint
H7338.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the dimension of width of a surface or space — what extends from one side to the other. It is a concrete, physical measure: we talk about the width of a road, a field, or any space.
2. It then describes a large open and clear expanse, a vast horizon. In Job 38:18, the reader is asked: "Have you comprehended the breadth of the earth?" — the image is that of the splendor of the created world, with its immense horizons.
3. Finally, the word takes on a figurative sense: width becomes a symbol of freedom and breathing space. In Job 36:16, God promises to take the righteous "out of distress, to set you at large, in full freedom" — it is the image of one being freed from chains, given space to breathe and move.
H7338.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root רחב (r-ch-b), which expresses the idea of opening, enlarging, extending. This same root produces other words: רחוב (street, wide public way) and the adjective רחב (wide, spacious). The underlying image is one of expansion, of space opening up and giving freedom.
H7338.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the Book of Job. In the first instance (Job 36:16), it expresses the freedom that God grants to the righteous after tribulation — it is a deliverance where one moves from confinement to open space. In the second (Job 38:18), it describes the immensity of creation, the vast world that only God knows in all its depth. Both uses associate width and greatness: either the greatness of divine creation or the breadth of grace that liberates.
H7338.portee: This word reminds us that authentic freedom, for the believer, comes from God alone. Being taken out of distress and set "at large" means that faith is not a prison, but a space where one can breathe, hope, and live fully. The image of the breadth of the earth also invites trust: the one who created this immense world is capable of guiding us wisely.

sens: An open passage between the houses of a city or village, where people circulate
A place for public gathering and assembly, courtyard or esplanade in a city
Figurative sense: the public domain, social and collective life
H7339.detail:
1. The street is primarily an urban circulation space, a path between dwellings: Lot offers his visitors to spend the night "in the street" (Genesis 19:2) rather than seeking a proper lodging, suggesting they might stay outside in the heart of the city. It is the place where people come and go, where daily traffic circulates.
2. The word also designates an open space where the community gathers for important public acts: King Hezekiah "gathered the people in the square" (2 Chronicles 32:6) to encourage them for battle, or the crowd gathered there to hear the Law read aloud (Nehemiah 8:1 and 8:3). It is a public square, a civic center.
3. Figuratively, the street symbolizes public life, the domain of the outside world: Wisdom "cries out in the streets" (Proverbs 1:20) to reach all the inhabitants; disasters unfold there — "all her warriors shall perish in the streets" (Jeremiah 50:30) expresses the collapse of the people.
H7339.origine: The Hebrew word רְחוֹב (rechov) comes from a root meaning "wide" or "spacious": it designates first something open and ample. That is why it is translated sometimes as "street" (linear passage space), sometimes as "square" (open and spacious area). The underlying image is that of free space, without enclosures, contrasting with the interiors of houses or private courtyards.
H7339.emploi: This word appears 41 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical, wisdom, and prophetic books. In the narratives (Genesis, Judges, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles), the street or square is the theater of daily urban life: it is where people meet, where they address the community. Proverbs and Isaiah place moral images there: Wisdom cries out there, or the guilty expose themselves. The prophets Jeremiah and Ezekiel use the word to describe ruins and public mourning — the street becomes the place of collective distress. Zechariah returns to it as a symbol of restored peace: "The streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls" (Zechariah 8:5).
H7339.portee: This word invites us to see the street and the square as places where the people meet, gather, and confront common reality. It symbolizes public and collective life, as opposed to the secret or the private. For the believer, it is a reminder that wisdom must be proclaimed openly, and that God's judgment is exercised over the whole people, not just in secret: the street is the place where truth is revealed and where everyone is seen.

sens: City in the territory of Asher, in northern Canaan
H7340G.detail: Rehob is a city mentioned in the allocation of territory among the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan. It is located in the north, not far from the Mediterranean coast and Sidon, and was assigned to the tribe of Asher (Joshua 19:28).
H7340G.origine: The Hebrew name Rehob literally means "wide place" or "spacious place," formed from the root that designates space or opening. It is a common geographical name in Canaan, likely designating a crossroads or an open area.
H7340G.emploi: Rehob appears only once in the canonical Bible, in the passage of Joshua 19:28 that lists the cities of the lot of the tribe of Asher. It is cited between Hammon and Kana, all three located in northern Canaan near Sidon. This context shows that Rehob was an established locality of the Asherite territory, likely a landmark in the land distribution system after the conquest.

sens: City of the tribe of Asher, in the Promised Land
Open or wide place (meaning of the name)
H7340H.detail:
1. Rehob is a city that was assigned to the tribe of Asher during the division of the Promised Land. It is mentioned in the list of cities of this tribe (Joshua 19:30), and then it becomes a Levitical city, meaning it was reserved for the priests of the family of Aaron (Joshua 21:31). In the time of the Judges, it was part of the lands that Asher did not fully conquer (Judges 1:31).
2. The name "Rehob" means "wide place" or "open place" in Hebrew, an image evoking a freely accessible space — which was common for city names in the region.
H7340H.origine: The Hebrew word רְחוֹב comes from a root meaning "to be wide" or "to extend." This name describes an open place, characteristic of cities in the Levant, and fits into the ancient custom of naming places after their visible geographical features. The word relates to the biblical geography of the ancient Near East.
H7340H.emploi: Rehob is mentioned four times in the provided biblical texts, all dating from the classical period of Israel (Joshua and Judges). It first appears in the official list of cities of Asher that were conquered or to be conquered (Joshua 19:30), then in the list of Levitical cities given to the descendants of Aaron (Joshua 21:31 and 1 Chronicles 6:75), making it a religious center. The account in Judges reveals that despite its official assignment, the tribe of Asher did not expel all the Canaanite inhabitants from this city and its surroundings (Judges 1:31), showing the limit of the northern conquest.

sens: father of King Hadadezer of Zobah
man of high rank during the united monarchy
figure of the ancient Near East in conflict with David
H7340I.detail:
1. Rehob is the father of King Hadadezer, who rules over the region of Zobah (in the northeast of present-day Palestine). In these two verses of 2 Samuel 8, David fights and defeats Hadadezer, son of Rehob, and plunders him.

2. Although mentioned only briefly in the Bible, Rehob represents an important royal authority of the ancient Near East during the time of King David (circa 1000 B.C.), when the united monarchy of Israel dominated its neighbors.
H7340I.origine: The name Rehob means "wide place" or "spacious place" in Hebrew, derived from the root that evokes the idea of open space or enlargement. The same word has been used to designate several cities and places in Israel: a boundary region to the north of Canaan and cities in Asher. It is a name carrying a notion of breadth or extensive domain.
H7340I.emploi: Rehob appears only twice in the provided usages, in both occurrences of the same event recounted in 2 Samuel 8. He is presented as the father of Hadadezer, king of Zobah, whom David defeated when he restored his dominion toward the Euphrates. This context places Rehob during the time of David's expansion and the conquests of the king of Israel over neighboring kingdoms. The source definition also indicates that other figures and places bear this name in the Bible (a Levite during the time of Nehemiah, a territorial boundary of the spies, cities in Asher), but the provided usages focus solely on the father of Hadadezer.

sens: Levite who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah
H7340J.detail: Rehob is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, during the ceremony where the leaders of the people of Israel solemnly seal the covenant with God under the leadership of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:11). His name means "spacious place" or "large space" in Hebrew, but this etymological detail does not shed light on his historical role.
H7340J.origine: The name Rehob comes from the Hebrew rechov (רְחוֹב), which literally means "wide place" or "spacious street" — the image of an open, clear city. This same word also designated geographical places in the Old Testament: a northern boundary of the lands explored by the spies in Canaan, and two cities in the territory of Asher. The name was borne by several individuals at different periods in Israel's history.
H7340J.emploi: Rehob appears only once in the Scriptures, in Nehemiah 10:11, in the list of Levites and leaders of the people who affixed their seal to the document of the renewed covenant after the return from exile in Babylon. This solemn moment, reported in chapter 10 of Nehemiah, marks the reaffirmation of Israel's commitment to obey the Law of Moses. Rehob is among the witnesses of this collective commitment, indicating his status as a recognized spiritual or civil leader of the people at that time.

sens: Locality in northern Canaan, northern limit of the spies' exploration
Region of Syria northeast of Israel
H7340K.detail:
1. Rehob is a city in northern Canaan, mentioned as the boundary point reached by the spies that Moses sent to explore the promised land (Numbers 13:21). It was located on the road to Hamath, a prosperous region to the north. The name means "wide place" or "open place," perhaps evoking a clear area or an important crossroads.
2. Rehob also refers to a Syrian region inhabited during the time of King David. When the Ammonites rebelled against Israel, the Syrians of Rehob came to support them militarily, arrayed in battle alongside other neighboring peoples (2 Samuel 10:8). At that time, Rehob was a small independent Aramean principality.
H7340K.origine: The name Rehob comes from the Hebrew rəḥōv, which literally means "width" or "open place." The root evokes a clear expanse, a public space where one can move freely. This same term also appears in the name "Beth-Rehob" (Beth-Rehob), meaning "house of Rehob," possibly designating a main site or a larger territory.
H7340K.emploi: Rehob appears twice in the Bible under this name. First as the northern boundary reached by Moses' spies: it marked the extreme point of their reconnaissance of the promised territory, on the road to Hamath (Numbers 13:21). Then, during David's time, Rehob is mentioned as a small independent Aramean nation, capable of mobilizing its warriors to fight alongside Ammon against Israel (2 Samuel 10:8). These two usages suggest that Rehob was a strategic site in northern Canaan and Syria, known for its commercial or military importance.

sens: Dimension of a thing from side to side, measured perpendicular to its length
Extent, space that stretches over a surface
Extension, breadth of a quality or knowledge
H7341.detail:
1. Width is the measurement of a thing taken from side to side, perpendicular to its length. It is one of the three main dimensions of an object: along with length and height, it defines its shape and size. Genesis 6:15 describes the ark with "three hundred cubits in length, fifty cubits in width, and thirty cubits in height," showing how this word expresses the proportions of a structure. The objects of the Tabernacle, such as the altar or the table, are similarly defined by their width (Exodus 25:10, 25:23).
2. In the sense of extent or surface area, the word denotes the breadth of a zone, region, or place. Ezekiel frequently uses "width" to describe the spaces of the restored temple and its walls (Ezekiel 42:10), indicating how the rooms and courts extend across the land.
3. Rarely, the word appears figuratively to express the extension, breadth of a spiritual or mental quality: 1 Kings 4:29 states that God gave Solomon "wisdom and understanding in very great abundance," where "width" of heart symbolizes open-mindedness and deep understanding.
H7341.origine: The Hebrew word rochav comes from the root rachav, which expresses the idea of being wide, to extend, to open up. This root evokes the movement of expansion, something that broadens or stretches. The basic image is that of openness and space: a wide place is one that is not narrow, that allows for room. Related verbs in the Bible express enlargement and dilation, while the noun rochav denotes the stable and measurable state of what is wide.
H7341.emploi: This word appears 89 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in descriptive passages of buildings and sacred structures. It abounds in Exodus, where it measures the rooms of the Tabernacle and their accessories (Exodus 25:10, 25:23, 26:2); in Kings and Chronicles, where it defines the dimensions of Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 6:2-6); and especially in Ezekiel, where the prophet meticulously describes the restored Temple with its gates, chambers, and courts (Ezekiel 40-42, over 30 occurrences). Outside of these architectural descriptions, the word is used sparingly: it appears in Job 37:10 regarding the extent of frozen water, and more rarely in a figurative sense, as in 1 Kings 4:29 to express the breadth of Solomon's wisdom. Its usage reflects the biblical importance of measured detail and precision in the representation of spaces dedicated to God.
H7341.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God is a God of order and precision: the exact dimensions of the Tabernacle and the Temple are never left to chance. Every cubit counts. This invites us to see in the structure of the holy places an expression of divine harmony and mastery. When Ezekiel describes the restored Temple with mathematical precision, he symbolizes a renewed, perfect world, ordered according to God's wisdom. Finally, the rare use of the word in the sense of spiritual breadth (Solomon's wisdom) suggests that true greatness is measured not only in cubits but in width of heart and understanding.

sens: that extends over a great distance from side to side
ample, offering plenty of space
H7342G.detail:
1. This word describes what has a large dimension from side to side: a wide wall is a wall whose width is significant. It is the opposite of what is narrow or thin. In the reconstruction of Jerusalem, the wide wall mentioned in Nehemiah 3:8 is a remarkable element of the fortification that is pointed out by naming it this way — a section that stands out for its proportions.
2. Figuratively, the word can evoke the idea of ample, spacious: what is wide offers room, freedom of movement. The wide path evokes an open way.
H7342G.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of extending, taking up space. It is related to other Hebrew words describing breadth or extension. This root belongs to the family of concrete terms that denote physical and spatial dimensions.
H7342G.emploi: The word רָחָב (rachav) appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the context of the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem during Nehemiah's time. In Nehemiah 3:8 and 12:38, it designates a section of the wall characterized by its width. The Nehemiah mentions it as a distinctive landmark during the reconstruction and the consecration procession. The meaning remains constant: an observable and remarkable physical dimension.

sens: that extends over a large area, that has plenty of space
that is spacious, wide, ample
that extends widely, that is not constricted or limited
H7342H.detail:
1. The word first describes the physical extent of a place or region: a country, land, or terrain that covers a vast area. In Genesis 34:21, it is said that "the land is large enough for them" — there is enough room to accommodate newcomers without conflict.
2. It then qualifies what is spacious or ample: a wide breach, an expansive sea. In Psalms 104:25, the sea is described as "great and vast," dominating the landscape.
3. Also used to describe a great width or amplitude in the sense of extension in time or possibilities: the psalmist says "You have set me in a large place" (Psalms 119:45), evoking a freedom and expansion that is not only physical but also spiritual — a life freed from constraints.
H7342H.origine: The Hebrew word רָחָב (rachav) comes from a root that expresses the idea of widening and dilation — the image of what broadens and opens. It is found in related words from the same Semitic family. In the Greek Old Testament, it is often translated by Greek words expressing width or extent. The fundamental image is that of space opening up, not constricting.
H7342H.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the Old Testament, primarily to describe spaces and lands: countries, regions, the sea. It notably appears in relation to divine promises — the land that God gives to Israel is "vast" and generous (Nehemiah 9:35, Exodus 3:8). It is also found in poetic descriptions and in laments: a "wide" breach is an opening that exposes to assault (Job 30:14). The word can also express a certain amplitude of life or understanding: "You have set me in a large place" (Psalms 119:45) means a spiritual dilation, a new freedom given by the Word of God.
H7342H.portee: This word invites the reader to contemplate the breadth of God's gifts — His generosity in Creation and in the promises made to His people. It also reminds us that the Word of God expands the soul and opens new horizons: it frees from narrowness and constraint. It is a word of comfort for those who feel confined or oppressed.

sens: having a wide, spacious, expandable heart
showing pride, arrogance, disdain towards others
reflecting pride and self-sufficiency
H7342I.detail: 1. The word first evokes the concrete image of wide and spacious: something that extends, takes up space, and expands. This is the very root of the word. 2. When applied to the heart or the gaze, it describes someone whose heart has 'swelled' with pride, who believes they are above others. In Proverbs 21:4, 'haughty eyes' and 'a heart that swells' denote this pride that refuses to bow before God or others. 3. The proud person is one who feels in control, who submits to no one, whose attitude creates conflicts. In Proverbs 28:25, 'the proud stirs up strife': their heart swollen with pride pushes them to impose their will on others.
H7342I.origine: The Hebrew word רָחָב (rachav) comes from a root meaning 'to be wide, spacious'. Its proper sense is purely physical: a wide place, a spacious road. But the Bible applies it to the heart or attitude to describe one who considers themselves important, whose pride 'takes up space'. The image is of a heart that expands, swelling with self-sufficiency — the opposite of a humble and contracted heart before God.
H7342I.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, exclusively in the book of Proverbs, and always in the figurative sense of pride or arrogance. In Proverbs 21:4, it qualifies the gaze and heart of the wicked: these 'haughty eyes' express their disdain and refusal to acknowledge God. In Proverbs 28:25, it designates the proud person themselves, whose proud attitude provokes conflicts around them. In both cases, pride is presented as a source of evil: it corrupts the heart and disturbs peace.
H7342I.portee: For the believer, this word reminds of the danger of spiritual pride: believing oneself to be above others, or worse, above God's commandments. Proverbs shows that pride is incompatible with wisdom and peace. It is a call to humility: to let one's heart contract rather than swell with pride.

sens: Woman of Jericho who welcomed the Israelite spies
Prostitute who hid the messengers of Israel
Mother of Boaz, ancestor of King David and Jesus
H7343.detail:
1. Rahab is a woman living in Jericho before the monarchy of Israel. When Joshua sends two spies to explore the city, they take refuge in her house (Joshua 2:1), showing that she was known and could be a hiding place.

2. She practiced the profession of a prostitute, a job carried out in the public space of Jericho. Despite this situation, she recognizes the God of Israel and risks her life by hiding the spies under flax stalks on her roof, defying the king's order demanding their surrender (Joshua 2:3 and 6:17).

3. For her act of courage and faith, she is saved with her entire family during the destruction of Jericho (Joshua 6:23, 25). She joins the people of Israel and becomes the wife of Salmon, giving birth to Boaz, who will become the grandfather of King David — making Rahab an ancestor of Jesus himself.
H7343.origine: The name Rahab means 'wide' or 'spacious' in Hebrew, perhaps alluding to her hospitality or open character. She is one of the few non-Israelite women named in the genealogy of Jesus, alongside Ruth, Bathsheba, and Mary. Scripture primarily remembers her for her act of faith: that is why the epistle of James cites her as an example of justification by works of faith (James 2:25).
H7343.emploi: Rahab appears in the five passages of Joshua 2 and 6, all recounting the same event: her welcoming of the spies, the king's conspiracy against her, her rescue during the ruin of Jericho, and her definitive integration into Israel. She symbolizes conversion: from foreigner and sinner, she becomes a member of God's people through faith. She reappears in the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew 1:5, and James 2:25 praises her for justifying her faith by her works. Her story shows that God can save anyone who believes in Him, regardless of their past or origin.
H7343.portee: Rahab teaches Christians that true faith changes a life: she not only believed in God, she acted by risking everything for the servants of the Lord. Her integration into Israel and into the lineage of Jesus proclaims that God excludes no one from His love and plan of salvation — neither the woman with a shameful past, nor the foreigner, nor the prostitute. She is a model of repentance and commitment.

sens: Well dug by Isaac in Philistine territory
Place where Isaac found peace after disputes
H7344G.detail:
1. Rehoboth is a well that the patriarch Isaac dug in the land of the Philistines, after leaving Gerar. It is the third well he undertakes to dig in this region (Genesis 26:22).

2. The name means 'spacious places' or 'wide spaces' in Hebrew: Isaac chose it to celebrate the fact that God had finally given him space and freedom, without the Philistines disputing him as they had for the two previous wells. It is a well of peace and deliverance.
H7344G.origine: The name Rehoboth comes from the Hebrew rechov, which designates a place, a street, or an open space. Isaac named the well to symbolize that after conflicts and expulsions, the Lord finally granted him space and prosperity. The name expresses the biblical idea that God liberates and enlarges the space of those who trust Him.
H7344G.emploi: Rehoboth is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 26:22, during the account of the wells dug by Isaac. This well holds symbolic importance in the patriarchal history: after the shepherds of Gerar disputed Isaac over the wells of Esek and Sitna, Rehoboth marks the moment when Isaac finally finds a place without conflict. Isaac publicly recognizes the blessing of the Lord who establishes him in the land with prosperity.
H7344G.portee: This story of Rehoboth teaches that divine blessing brings not only material goods but also peace, the space to live and prosper without oppression. For the believing reader, it shows how perseverance in trusting God leads from conflict to peace and from narrowness to freedom.

sens: City in Arabia, between Mesopotamia and the land of Edom
H7344H.detail: Rehoboth is a city in the desert region between Mesopotamia and Edom, from which Saul (or Shaul), one of the ancient kings of Edom, originated. The name literally means 'wide places' or 'wide streets' in Hebrew, perhaps evoking an open place in the desert. It is mentioned as the city from which Saul ruled, located near a river (probably the Euphrates or the Tigris according to the geographical context of ancient Edom). The only two biblical mentions locate it in this historical region of the ancient Near East.
H7344H.origine: The Hebrew name Rehoboth (רְחֹבוֹת) comes from the root רחב (r.ch.b) meaning 'wide, open space'. The plural 'rchoboth' (wide places) suggests a city characterized by its open spaces or squares, an appropriate image for a desert city. This type of descriptive name was common in antiquity to designate places.
H7344H.emploi: Rehoboth appears twice in the Bible, always in relation to Saul, king of Edom. In Genesis 36:37 and 1 Chronicles 1:48 (parallel passages), it is presented as the city from which Saul reigned after Samla. These texts are part of the genealogical list of the ancient kings of Edom, before the monarchy of Israel. Rehoboth is described as being 'by the river', indicating an important location in the historical geography of the Edomite and Mesopotamian region.

sens: ancient city of Mesopotamia, one of the four cities founded by Asshur near Nineveh
H7344I.detail: 1. Rehoboth is a city built by Asshur, the founding and eponymous figure of the Assyrian empire. The name literally means "broad places" or "wide streets" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of a spacious and well-organized city. It is listed among the four great cities attributed to Asshur (Genesis 10:11).
H7344I.origine: The Hebrew word רְחֹבוֹת (rehoboth) comes from the root רְחַב (rechab) which means "wide" or "spacious." The plural "broad places" suggests a city with open spaces, typical of significant fortified cities in Mesopotamia. The biblical text mentions Rehoboth alongside Nineveh, Calah, and Hir, all of which were major in Assyrian history.
H7344I.emploi: Rehoboth appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 10:11. This passage lists the cities founded or conquered by Asshur during his expansion in Mesopotamia. The mention of Rehoboth in this genealogical list connects Assyrian history to the origins of the peoples described at the beginning of Genesis. Although the biblical text is brief about this city, it is known through archaeology as an important Assyrian administrative and religious center.

sens: Levite from the desert period, only son of Eliezer and grandson of Moses
H7345.detail: Rechabia is a member of the tribe of Levi who lived during the time of the Exodus and in the desert. He is the only son of Eliezer, who himself was the son of Moses. Although Rechabia does not have many personal children mentioned, it is notable that his descendants formed an important lineage among the Levites: in 1 Chronicles 23:17, we learn that "Rechabia" was the head of his family branch and that "the sons of Rechabia were very numerous." He appears in genealogical lists and the organization of Levitical offices, notably in 1 Chronicles 24:21 where his family receives a defined priestly charge.
H7345.origine: The name literally means "Jehovah has enlarged," composed of the Hebrew God (Yah) and the verb "to enlarge" (rachab). This name evokes the idea that God granted a numerous offspring and a blessing to this family. The family connection is remarkable: Rechabia is the grandson of the prophet Moses through his mother, making his lineage a prominent genealogical branch in the history of Israel.
H7345.emploi: Rechabia appears three times in the book of Chronicles, always in the context of genealogies and the organization of the Levites during the reign of King David. In 1 Chronicles 23:17, he is presented as the head of his family and father of a numerous offspring. In 1 Chronicles 24:21, his family is recorded among the Levitical divisions responsible for temple service. In 1 Chronicles 26:25, he appears in the descending genealogy, showing how his line has continued through several generations (Rechabia, Isaiah, Joram, Zicri, Shelomith). These mentions reflect the administrative and religious importance of his family in the organization of Israelite worship.

sens: Son of Solomon and first king of Judah after the division of the kingdom of Israel
H7346.detail: Roboam is the son of Solomon and Naamah. Upon his father's death, he becomes king of Judah (1 Kings 11:43 and 2 Chronicles 9:31). His reign is marked by the great schism of the unified kingdom: the ten northern tribes rebel against him and form the kingdom of Israel under Jeroboam, while Roboam retains only the kingdom of Judah (1 Kings 12:17-18 and 2 Chronicles 10:17). Despite this territorial loss, he strengthens the defenses of Judah and fortifies several cities (1 Kings 14:27 and 2 Chronicles 11:5).
H7346.origine: The name "Roboam" means "a people has enlarged" or "he whose people has enlarged," perhaps reflecting the hope of dynastic expansion. It is a typical Hebrew name, composed of elements meaning "people" and "to enlarge." Roboam bears the name of his ancestor in a royal lineage that embodies the promises made to David.
H7346.emploi: Roboam appears 41 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the Books of Kings and Chronicles, which detail his accession to the throne, the division of the kingdom, and his subsequent reigns. He is portrayed as a politically weak king: he refuses the counsel of the elders and chooses to listen to the young who advise him harshly, thus provoking the revolt of the ten tribes (1 Kings 12:6-12 and 2 Chronicles 10:6-12). His story illustrates the instability of the unified kingdom and the consequences of poor political decisions.
H7346.portee: The story of Roboam teaches that power and prestige, even inherited from the greatest king of his time, do not guarantee success if the leader lacks wisdom and humility. His inability to heed the counsel of the wise and his pride lead to the division of the kingdom and the loss of ten tribes, illustrating how arrogance and lack of discernment result in lasting consequences.

sens: round and flat stone used for grinding grains
one of the two stones that form this device
daily working tool, symbol of domestic life and labor
H7347.detail:
1. A millstone is a large round and flat stone, often made of sandstone or limestone, used for grinding grains to produce flour. One stone is placed on top of the other, and the upper stone is rubbed against the lower stone while grains are poured between them. The text of Numbers 11:8 shows the Israelites who "ground" the manna "with millstones" — the action of grinding, reducing to powder.
2. Sometimes the Bible refers to one of the two stones in particular: Deuteronomy 24:6 mentions "the two millstones" and "the upper millstone," distinguishing the upper stone (the one that is operated) from the lower stone (fixed). This distinction had legal value: they could not be seized as collateral, as they were essential for the family's survival.
3. The millstone represents much more than just a tool: it is the heart of the household, the symbol of ordinary life, daily work, and domestic peace. Isaiah 47:2 and Jeremiah 25:10 use it to signify the total destruction of a civilization — when the millstones cease to turn, it indicates that normal life has disappeared, and famine and desolation reign.
H7347.origine: The Hebrew word recheh belongs to the family of verbs that mean "to grind" or "to crush." Its starting image is that of the mechanical, repeated action of reducing hard grains to fine powder. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this word was rendered by the Greek myle, which also means millstone. The instrument was universal in the ancient Near East: two simple stones, requiring no metal or complex technology, making it accessible to all.
H7347.emploi: The word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts related to domestic work, food, or daily life. Exodus 11:5 mentions it in the context of the tenth plague: even the servant who grinds grain will be struck. Numbers 11:8 describes the Israelites grinding the manna to make cakes. Deuteronomy 24:6 legally protects it, prohibiting the creditor from seizing it as collateral — it was a sacred possession. Isaiah 47:2 and Jeremiah 25:10 use it as an image of divine judgment: when the millstones stop turning, it is a sign of the end of the known world, the disappearance of civilized life.
H7347.portee: The millstone reminds Christians that God values ordinary and daily work: it is the instrument of simple people, of women who feed their families. It also shows how seemingly mundane elements are precious — the Bible protects them by law. Finally, its silence in the prophecies of judgment becomes eloquent: when God withdraws, it is not the palaces that cease to exist first, but the daily bread. It is an invitation not to take for granted the simple acts of life.

sens: Man who returned from exile with Zerubbabel
Levite from the family of Bani who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem
Leader of the people who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah
H7348A.detail: Rehum is the name of a man mentioned several times in the accounts of the return from exile and the rebuilding of Jerusalem. The first Rehum, cited in Ezra 2:2, is among those who return from Babylonian captivity with Zerubbabel and participate in the restoration of the people of Israel in their land. Another Rehum, mentioned in Nehemiah 12:3, is a Levite from the family of Bani who actively engages in the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership. This same man, or perhaps a third bearer of the name, is among the leaders of the people who seal Nehemiah's covenant, committing the restored community to follow the Law of the Lord.
H7348A.origine: The name Rehum means "compassion" in Hebrew, derived from a root that evokes mercy and tenderness. This name, borne by several men during the times of exile and return, reflects the spirit of kindness that God shows toward His exiled people.
H7348A.emploi: Rehum appears in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, which recount the return of the Judeans from exile in Babylon and the restoration of Jerusalem in the 5th century B.C. In Ezra 2:2, he is listed among the chief leaders who accompany Zerubbabel on his return. In Nehemiah 12:3, he is identified as a Levite participating in the rebuilding of the walls. These mentions show that Rehum played an important role in the communal and religious organization of the restored people, contributing both to the material reconstruction and to the spiritual life of the community.
H7348A.portee: The example of Rehum reminds readers that the restoration of God's people is not the work of a single individual, but of a united community where everyone, whether Levite or leader, contributes their commitment. His name, evoking compassion, invites recognition that the return from exile is a manifestation of God's mercy toward His people.

sens: Persian governor in the service of King Artaxerxes
Adversary of the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem
H7348B.detail:
1. Réhum is a Persian governor who exercises authority in Samaria and the surrounding regions during the time of exile and return (Ezra 4:8). His title and administrative function make him an influential figure at the royal court.
2. He actively opposes the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem: along with his secretary Shimshai and other colleagues, he writes to King Artaxerxes a letter against this project (Ezra 4:8). Once the king's response is received, he intervenes to halt the work "by force and violence" (Ezra 4:23), thus embodying the political and administrative resistance to the restoration of Jewish worship.
H7348B.origine: The name Réhum means "compassion" in Hebrew, but this meaning does not manifest in the character of the figure as described in the biblical text. He belongs to the Persian period of Israel's history (after the Babylonian exile, in the 5th century B.C.).
H7348B.emploi: Réhum appears four times in the book of Ezra, always in chapter 4, in the account of the return and reconstruction. He is presented as governor (Ezra 4:8, 4:17) acting in concert with Shimshai, the secretary. His role unfolds in two phases: first, drafting the letter of protest to the king (Ezra 4:8-9), and then executing the royal order that halts the work (Ezra 4:23). He represents the local administrative authority that, for political reasons, opposes the restoration of the Jewish people in Jerusalem.
H7348B.portee: Réhum illustrates how external obstacles and worldly powers can block God's plans. His story reminds believers that the reconstruction of the temple and the restoration of the people faced real human resistance, and that only God's intervention (through a change of king or policy) ultimately allowed the work to continue. It is a call to perseverance in faith in the face of obstacles.

sens: Levite who participated in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile
H7348G.detail: Rehum is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the Jewish people return from the Babylonian exile. He is the son of Bani and participated in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership, around the mid-5th century B.C. His name means "compassion" in Hebrew, which recalls God's mercy toward His people during this period of restoration.
H7348G.origine: The name Rehum comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to have pity" or "to show compassion." It is a theophoric name, meaning it expresses a divine quality — mercy — that parents attributed to their child or hoped for from God for him. This root appears in several biblical names and evokes God's compassionate goodness.
H7348G.emploi: Rehum appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:17. He is presented among the workers and leaders who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem after the return from exile. This list in Nehemiah 3 enumerates the different groups (priests, Levites, laypeople) and the sections of the wall that each built. Rehum is listed as an active Levite in this great national and religious restoration effort.
H7348G.portee: The mention of Rehum, even briefly, reminds the reader that the reconstruction of Jerusalem involved many obscure workers, of whom only a few names have reached us. It illustrates how God raised up His people to restore what had been destroyed, and how each person, from the greatest to the humblest, had a part in this work. It is an invitation to recognize that every work of spiritual restoration requires the concrete commitment of many faithful individuals.

sens: Figure from the time of exile and return
Leader who opposed the reconstruction of Jerusalem
H7348H.detail: Réhum is a man mentioned in the Bible at the time of the return from exile, when the Israelites were rebuilding Jerusalem. His name means "compassion" in Hebrew, but his actions show a very different attitude: he wrote a letter to King Artaxerxes to oppose the project of rebuilding the holy city (Nehemiah 10:25). He represents those who sought to hinder the work of restoring Jerusalem.
H7348H.origine: The name Réhum comes from the Hebrew rechum, derived from the root rahm, which means "to have compassion" or "to show mercy." It is a name with a positive meaning, but whose bearer does not reflect this meaning in his actions: he opposes the divine project of restoration. The name is regularly formed from the verb meaning "to have pity"; it appears in other Hebrew names of the same family.
H7348H.emploi: Réhum appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:25. He is cited among those who signed the solemn commitment of the people to respect God's Law upon their return from exile. He is a very brief figure in the biblical text, but illustrates the tensions of the return period: some among the local political authorities opposed the restoration of Jerusalem and its walls.

sens: One who feels compassion, pity towards those who suffer
One who acts with gentleness and indulgence towards the weak and sinners
A prominent characteristic of God: His tenderness in the face of human misery
H7349.detail:
1. The word describes one who feels compassion in the face of another's suffering — an emotion that drives one to help and console. It is the heart moved by distress. Only God is truly presented this way in the Bible: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and compassionate, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6).
2. The word also expresses a gentle and indulgent way of acting: God does not destroy those who plead with Him, but lifts them up. "In your great mercy, you do not completely destroy them or abandon them, for you are a God compassionate and gracious" (Nehemiah 9:31).
3. It is a fundamental divine quality, which recurs throughout the Psalms and prayers: "The LORD is merciful and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love" (Psalms 145:8). It reassures the believer who knows they can rely on this divine pity.
H7349.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "belly," "seat of deep emotion." Like other Hebrew terms, it denotes an intense, visceral emotion. In Hebrew, "mercy" arises from the belly, the deepest heart — which makes the term very vivid and embodied. The adjective is formed from this verb to express one who naturally possesses this tenderness.
H7349.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always to describe God — with only one possible exception. It first appears in the solemn declaration of Exodus 34:6, where God reveals Himself to Moses after the sin of the golden calf: it is His very nature. The psalmist regularly uses it to praise God (Psalms 86:15; 111:4; 145:8), and Nehemiah uses it to remind the exiled people that God has not completely abandoned them (Nehemiah 9:17, 9:31). Jonah uses it to acknowledge God's compassion towards Nineveh (Jonah 4:2). This word especially recurs in moments when the believer doubts, sins, or suffers: it comes to reassure them about God's unwavering character.
H7349.portee: Understanding that God is compassionate — and not just just or holy — changes everything for the distressed believer. It means that God sees our suffering, is moved by it, and does not abandon those who return to Him, even after infidelity. This divine quality underpins confident prayer and sincere repentance: God does not crush us under His judgment, but lifts us up with tenderness.

sens: At a great distance in space
At a great distance in time
(Adjective) Located at a great distance
Extent, interval that separates two things
Absence, moral or spiritual separation
H7350.detail:
1. The word first describes a spatial separation: Abraham sees the place of sacrifice "from afar" (Genesis 22:4), meaning at a distance. The servants of Joshua come from a very "distant" land (Joshua 9:9), located far from Israel. It is the concrete image of distance that one measures by foot or sight.
2. The word also applies to time: God has prepared events "from afar," meaning a long time ago, before the present generations were born (Isaiah 37:26). The interval between the past and the present is described as a distance to be crossed.
3. Used as an adjective, it qualifies what is "distant" or "far away": the "distant lands," the "far-off peoples" to which God draws the children of Israel (Isaiah 60:4). It is a permanent quality of what lies beyond the horizon.
4. As a noun, the word designates the gap itself, the "distance" as an abstract measure: Joshua commands the people to keep a certain distance behind the ark (Joshua 3:4).
5. Figuratively, the word expresses a spiritual separation: "salvation is far from the wicked" (Psalms 119:155) means they are deprived of it, that it is not accessible to them. Likewise, God is not "far" from the heart of one who seeks Him (Jeremiah 23:23).
H7350.origine: The Hebrew word רָחֹק comes from a root that evokes the idea of stretching out, moving away. In the Hebrew Bible, it is one of the most common terms to express physical distance. The corresponding Aramaic word, רְחִיק, carries the same meaning. This root emphasizes that distance is not simply static: it is a separation created by spreading out or the interval.
H7350.emploi: The word appears 84 times in the Segond 1910, mainly in Isaiah, the Psalms, and historical narratives. In the historical narratives (Genesis, Joshua, Judges), it describes tangible geographical distances. In the Psalms and the prophets, it gains a spiritual dimension: distance symbolizes lack, deprivation, or waiting. Sometimes it qualifies peoples or lands ("distant peoples"), sometimes it forms an adverbial expression ("from afar"), and sometimes it is the subject of a judgment ("salvation is far"). The context determines whether it refers to a real distance, a temporal interval, or a moral separation.
H7350.portee: This word invites reflection on spiritual distance: it can express the absence of God who seems "far" in times of distress (Psalms 22:2), but also the love of God that embraces those who are "far" (Jeremiah 31:3). By reminding us that God prepares His work "from afar," the word affirms His foreknowledge and mastery of time. For the believer, it highlights that closeness to God depends less on geography than on the orientation of the heart.

sens: Board or beam that covers the ceiling or walls of a house
Luxury woodwork, noble or crafted material
Interior ornamentation of a dwelling
H7351.detail:
1. Paneling is primarily a board or beam fixed to the ceiling or walls to cover and decorate them. The Song of Solomon 1:17 speaks of "beams" (the supporting beams) and "paneling" (the visible covering) in cedar and cypress: the word thus designates the visible woodwork that adorns the interior of the house.
2. By extension, paneling evokes luxury and the quality of the materials used. In Israel, using cedar or cypress for this was a mark of wealth and refinement, reserved for royal houses or affluent dwellings. This is why the text lists these precious woods: it aims to show the splendor and value of what is covered.
3. Paneling also represents the ornamentation and embellishment of a house, making it pleasant to see and inhabit. In the context of the Song, it contributes to the poetic image of a beautiful and elegant dwelling.
H7351.origine: The Hebrew word רָהִיט (rehit) literally means a board or strip of wood. It comes from a root that means "to arrange" or "to set in order." The family of words related to this root evokes the idea of arrangement and organization. The context of the Song shows that it refers to a covering woodwork, hence the choice of the word "paneling" in English, which corresponds exactly to this type of visible panel or beam that adorns interiors.
H7351.emploi: The word rehit appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 1:17. It is used to describe the luxurious interior of a house, associated with the most precious materials of the time: cedar and cypress. The context is one of a poetic celebration of the beauty and richness of a dwelling, which serves as a backdrop for the expression of love and intimacy. This unique occurrence reveals that the word is indeed a term of interior architecture, designating precisely the covering of surfaces.
H7351.portee: This word invites contemplation of the beauty of created things and the value that the Bible recognizes in the embellishment of a house. In the Song, the luxury and order of the woodwork are not condemned, but celebrated as an expression of abundance and joy of living. It reminds us that creating beauty around oneself is a form of wisdom and appreciation of God's gifts.

sens: At a distance, separated by space
Distant, remote
H7352.detail: 1. This word denotes what is separated by a notable distance. In Ezra 6:6, the Persian king orders the governors to stay "far" from the temple construction site, meaning not to approach it, to maintain a distance from the place. 2. More broadly, it qualifies what is far away, distant, having a great distance between oneself and another thing. It is the opposite of what is near or in proximity.
H7352.origine: This Aramaic word comes from a parallel Hebrew root (רָחֹק, rahoq) which also means "distant" or "far." The family of words expresses the idea of spatial remoteness or separation. The basic image is that of a distance that separates two things or two people.
H7352.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible: in Ezra 6:6, where a royal decree in Aramaic orders the authorities of the territory beyond the river to stay far from the reconstruction site of the Jerusalem temple. It is an order of non-interference in the religious affairs of the Jews.
H7352.portee: This term reminds us that obstacles and distances can be imposed by human authorities, but cannot stop God's plan. Even "far" from the temple, the people continue the work of its reconstruction.

sens: Female sheep, animal raised for its wool and meat
Flock of sheep
Gentle and docile nature of the sheep
Image of the innocent or the oppressed faithful
H7353.detail:
1. The sheep is the female of the ram. It is a domesticated animal raised in flocks to provide wool, milk, and meat. In the Bible, the patriarchs and shepherds owned large flocks of sheep (Genesis 31:38: Jacob lists his sheep among his possessions after twenty years of work).

2. The word also refers to the entire flock or a group of sheep. Laban offered Jacob two hundred sheep and twenty rams (Genesis 32:14), showing that the word can encompass several individuals.

3. The sheep evokes by its nature gentleness, innocence, and passive obedience. In Song of Solomon 6:6, the beloved's teeth are compared to a flock of sheep coming up from the washing: the image glorifies whiteness, order, and regular beauty.

4. The sheep symbolizes one who suffers without resisting, particularly in prophetic texts. In Isaiah 53:7, the suffering servant is presented as a silent sheep before those who shear it: he does not defend himself, does not protest, going to death with submission. This image anchors the Passion of Christ in the Old Testament.
H7353.origine: The Hebrew word rāḥēl literally means "female sheep": it evokes an image of gentleness and tenderness. Rachel embodies beauty and grace in the patriarchal narrative: she is described as "beautiful in form and appearance" (Genesis 29:17). She is Jacob's beloved, for whom he agrees to work fourteen years in total.
H7353.emploi: The word appears four times in the Segond, always in the concrete sense of a domesticated animal. Genesis 31:38 and 32:14 use "sheep" in an economic and pastoral context: Jacob lists his sheep as part of his wealth and flock. In Song of Solomon 6:6, the word serves as a flattering poetic comparison. In Isaiah 53:7, a central prophetic location, the sheep becomes an image of submission and innocence in the face of violence, representing one who does not resist his fate. The concrete meaning remains present, but is enriched with symbolic depth according to the context.
H7353.portee: The sheep reminds the Christian reader that Jesus was compared to this gentle and defenseless animal. Isaiah 53:7 reveals that the Messiah would go to death without crying out, without rebelling, like a silent sheep. This image sheds light on the meaning of the crucifixion: not a warrior's victory, but radical obedience and an accepted death for the forgiveness of sins. It also invites the believer to meditate on the innocence and trust that God requires.

sens: Wife of Jacob, mother of Joseph and Benjamin
Character in the patriarchal narrative
H7354.detail: Rachel is the younger daughter of Laban, encountered by Jacob at a well. She becomes his beloved: Jacob agrees to serve her father for seven years to marry her (Genesis 29:18). Although Jacob first marries Leah through Laban's trickery, he remains attached to Rachel, with whom he ultimately has two sons: Joseph and Benjamin (Genesis 35:24). Her life is marked by suffering — she remains barren for a long time before God remembers her and makes her fruitful (Genesis 30:22) — and she dies giving birth to Benjamin (Genesis 35:19).
H7354.origine: The Hebrew name רָחֵל (Rachel) means "ewe": it evokes an image of gentleness and tenderness. Rachel embodies beauty and grace in the patriarchal narrative: she is described as "beautiful in form and appearance" (Genesis 29:17). She is Jacob's beloved, for whom he agrees to work fourteen years in total.
H7354.emploi: Rachel appears more than 40 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in Genesis, at the heart of Jacob's narrative. She is first the daughter of the Syrian Laban (Genesis 29:6), then Jacob's cherished wife despite the prior marriage to her sister Leah. The tension between the two sisters manifests in their competition to bear children for Jacob (Genesis 30:1-8). Rachel as a mother becomes the figure of maternal pain: in Jeremiah 31:15, the prophet evokes her weeping for her children, an image of the people of Israel in captivity. She is also honored in Ruth 4:11 as an ancestor of the house of Israel.
H7354.portee: Rachel embodies faithful love and patience in suffering. Her story shows that barrenness, seen as a curse in the ancient world, depends only on God, who "remembers" her (Genesis 30:22). Mother of Joseph and Benjamin, she is the ancestor of the two most important tribes of Israel. Her destiny — true love, pain, and joy finally given by God — resonates with the divine promise to the patriarchs. For the believer, she reminds us that God hears the cries of the wounded heart and gives life to those who seem condemned to silence.

sens: To feel a deep tenderness, a benevolent love towards someone
To show pity, mercy towards one who suffers or has failed
To turn away from anger to grant favor and forgiveness
To provide help and restore one who has been punished
H7355.detail:
1. It is primarily the tender love of a parent for their child: Psalm 103:13 compares the compassion of the Lord to that of a father for his children — a natural and deep affection that springs from the heart.

2. It is also active pity: refusing to strike further, or sparing one who could be destroyed. In Hosea 2:6, the Lord says He will have no pity on the children born of prostitution — this means He will not spare them from the punishment they deserve.

3. It is mercy granted after judgment: in Isaiah 60:10, the Lord says to Jerusalem, "I struck you in my anger, but in my mercy I have compassion on you" — He withdraws His angry hand and turns towards her with kindness to restore her.

4. Finally, it is restoration and help: in Jeremiah 30:18, the prophet announces that the Lord will have compassion on Jacob by bringing back his captives, which means He will actively intervene to restore His people to their former condition.
H7355.origine: The verb comes from the root רחם (r-ch-m), which literally evokes maternal womb (the Hebrew word "rehem" refers to the uterus). From this derives the idea of visceral tenderness, an emotion that arises from the depths: compassion is a movement of the belly, not a cold decision. The word "rachmanim" (compassionate) and "rachamim" (compassions, mercies) belong to the same family. This is why in Hebrew, compassion is not an intellectual feeling, but an instinctive reaction of the heart in the face of misery.
H7355.emploi: This verb appears 43 times in the Old Testament, especially among the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah) and in the Psalms. It is constantly used to describe the Lord's attitude towards Israel: God "has compassion" despite the people's sin (Deuteronomy 30:3), He "has pity" after punishment to restore His children (Jeremiah 31:20), He "will show mercy" to those who fear Him (Psalms 103:13). But the verb can also be used negatively: the Lord can refuse His compassion to those who persist in evil (Hosea 2:6). It is a key word in the theology of repentance and restoration: it summarizes the heart of God, who prefers mercy over judgment (Isaiah 30:18).
H7355.portee: This word reveals the heart of the God of the Bible: He is not a detached and cold judge, but a God who "has bowels" of tenderness for His creatures. For the believer, it assures that divine judgment never has the final word — God prefers to restore and uplift one who turns to Him. It is a reason for confidence in prayer and repentance: to say "Have compassion on me" (as in Psalms 102:14) is to address a God whose very nature is to show grace.

sens: The mother's belly, the place where the fetus develops before birth
The pregnant woman or her fertility
That which gives birth or brings forth
Compassion, natural tenderness towards one whom one has borne
H7356A.detail:
1. The maternal womb primarily refers to the belly or lap of the mother, that intimate place where the child forms before birth. It is the most concrete image: Isaiah 46:3 speaks of those whom God has "carried from your birth," meaning since He conceived them in a way like a mother carries her child.
2. The word can also refer to the woman herself in her capacity to bear children, her fertility. Judges 5:30 mentions "young girls," where the word refers to age and reproductive ability: "One young girl, two young girls per man".
3. By extension, it signifies the act of giving birth, bringing forth, or even the intention to produce an effect. Ezekiel 20:26 speaks of defiling the people "by their offerings" — the word expresses the intention to punish, as if one were bringing forth a judgment.
4. Finally, the word carries the idea of compassion or tenderness, as it naturally arises in one who has borne a child. Genesis 49:25 names the "blessings of the breasts and of the maternal womb," meaning the blessings of fertility and maternal protection that God grants.
H7356A.origine: The Hebrew word racham comes from a root that evokes the uterus or maternal belly, this home of life. The same family of words has given rise to "rachamim" (סרחמים), the bowels or compassion, as the Hebrews saw in the bowels the seat of maternal tenderness — the love that drives one to protect that which one has borne. The Greek word "splanchnon" (bowels) often translates this idea of visceral compassion in Greek.
H7356A.emploi: The word appears five times in the Old Testament, in various contexts. Genesis 49:25 uses it to speak of the blessings of fertility that Jacob calls upon Ephraim and Manasseh. Judges 5:30 uses it to refer to young girls. Proverbs 30:16 lists what is never satisfied, including "the barren woman" — one who cannot bear children remains tormented by this lack. Isaiah 46:3 uses it figuratively: God says He has carried Israel "from your birth," like a mother carries her child, an image of protection and personal connection. Ezekiel 20:26 finally uses the word in a construction where it signifies intention or desire: "I wanted to punish them this way." The meaning shifts from the biological organ to the notion of tenderness, generation, and intention.
H7356A.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that God knows His children intimately and personally, as a mother knows the one she has borne. It speaks of divine protection: Isaiah 46:3 shows a God who carries us as a mother carries her child, highlighting the relationship of love and deep commitment. It is also an invitation to turn towards compassion (the related word "rachamim") towards those who suffer, as this tenderness naturally springs up within us.

sens: Natural tenderness, emotion in response to the suffering of others
Pity and kindness towards those who suffer or are in need
Divine mercy, God's prompt forgiveness towards sinners
Grace given without it being deserved
Deep feeling of love towards someone
H7356B.detail:
1. The word first denotes a visceral reaction to misery: it is literally an emotion of the "bowels," the seat of tenderness in ancient Hebrew. When Genesis 43:30 recounts that Joseph "was moved with compassion" upon seeing Benjamin, it describes a profound emotional shock that seized him.
2. It manifests in concrete actions: it is active pity that drives one to help. David asks God to make him "find compassion" in the sight of Pharaoh (Genesis 43:14), meaning a kindness that translates into acts of favor.
