3. In relation to God, the word denotes His mercy: the Lord's attitude towards rebellious and guilty Israel. Lamentations 3:22 proclaims that "the Lord's mercies are not consumed" — even after punishment, there remains forgiveness.
4. It is also the unmerited, free grace: God grants His compassions not because they are earned, but because He Himself is compassionate (Nehemiah 9:31).
5. The word can finally express deep affection: the visceral bond between the one who has compassion and the one who receives it, a feeling that unites them.
H7356B.origine: The word comes from a root that literally means "bowels" or "womb" (the seat of life and tenderness). The Hebrew root רחם (rachèm) evokes intimate warmth, maternal affection. The Psalms and Lamentations repeatedly use this word to implore God, basing their prayer on the image of a primordial, maternal tenderness that God carries within Himself. The word has an Aramaic equivalent (רַחֲמִין) found in the later passages of the Hebrew Bible.
H7356B.emploi: The word appears 39 times, mainly in the Psalms, Lamentations, and the prophetic books. It denotes sometimes human compassion (when Jacob seeks the compassion of the Egyptian vizier, Genesis 43:14; when Joseph is moved towards Benjamin, Genesis 43:30), but more often and predominantly divine mercy — this is its dominant usage. God is called "compassionate and merciful" (Nehemiah 9:31; implicit in Exodus). The word is enriched in contexts of repentance: Israel in exile or distress pleads with God to remember His compassions (Lamentations 3:22; Psalms 79:8; Psalms 103:4). It also appears in exhortations to justice: Zechariah 7:9 calls for "mercy and compassion" towards the widow and the orphan.
H7356B.portee: This word teaches us that God is not a cold and unyielding judge, but a Father who suffers with us in our suffering. It invites us to recognize that all divine forgiveness is free, based not on our merits but on God's eternal tenderness. For the reader, it becomes a call to imitate this compassion towards others: exercising mercy is not a legal duty, but a participation in the very heart of God.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, son of Shema
H7357.detail: Racham is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, as a genealogical link in the lineage of Caleb. He is the son of Shema and the father of Jorkeam (1 Chronicles 2:44). His role is purely genealogical: the Bible cites him to establish the descent of Caleb's clan during the divided monarchy, without recounting any events of his life.
H7357.origine: The name Racham means "womb" in Hebrew, derived from the root רחם (racham) which evokes the uterus or maternal breast, and thus compassion and pity (roots of maternal love). Here, as often in biblical names, it simply designates a person without the meaning of the name being explained to us.
H7357.emploi: Racham appears only once in Scripture (1 Chronicles 2:44), in the genealogy of the descendants of Judah and Caleb. He lived during the divided monarchy. His sole mention situates him as the father of a lineage that has continued in the tribe of Judah, without any personal details being provided.

sens: the womb of the mother, place where the child forms before birth
sterility or inability to conceive
the act or power of conceiving and giving birth
the firstborn, children born from the mother's womb
H7358.detail:
1. The womb refers to the maternal belly, the place where the child forms before birth. This is the most concrete image of the word: Job asks why he was not dead "in the womb of his mother" (Job 3:11), and Jeremiah recalls that God knew him "before you were formed in the womb" (Jeremiah 1:5).
2. The word can also denote sterility, the inability to conceive children: God had struck "the whole house of Abimelech with barrenness" (Genesis 20:18), meaning He closed the wombs of the women.
3. By extension, it can signify the act or power of giving birth: Rachel weeps because her womb does not bear children, then "God remembered Rachel" and she conceived (Genesis 30:22).
4. The word also refers to the firstborn, those who have opened their mother's womb: "I offer as a sacrifice to the Lord every firstborn male" (Exodus 13:15) refers to those who have come out of the womb.
H7358.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of maternal tenderness and pity. The family of this word includes terms related to mercy and maternal love, as the womb is the closest bond between mother and child. This is why God is often described as having pity (a neighboring root) towards His people, like a mother towards her children.
H7358.emploi: This word appears 25 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books (Genesis, Exodus, Numbers), the Psalms, and the prophets. It primarily denotes literally the maternal womb: Genesis recounts the opening of the wombs (the first conceptions), and Exodus speaks of the firstborn who come out of the womb. It is also used for female sterility (Genesis 20:18, 1 Samuel 1:5-6): this is a terrible misfortune in biblical culture, as without children, a woman has no future. Job and Jeremiah use it to express the anguish of birth: Job regrets not having died at birth (Job 3:11), and Jeremiah curses the day he was conceived (Jeremiah 20:17). The passages in Exodus about the firstborn show that this word can also refer to children born from the womb.
H7358.portee: This word reminds us that God knows each person from before their birth, from their formation in the womb (Jeremiah 1:5). It also evokes the deep and unique bond between a mother and her child, reflecting God's tenderness. For the believer, it is an assurance that their life is not a coincidence, but that it has been thought of and known by God from the very beginning.

sens: action of demanding insistently
urgent call addressed to someone to take action
H7359.detail:
1. The word refers to the act of demanding forcefully and urgently. In Daniel 2:18, it is about 'committing' God, meaning to urgently plead with Him, to press Him to intervene. It is not a simple quiet prayer, but an insistent call, almost a passionate supplication.
2. It is also the act of imploring someone on behalf of a cause. Daniel and his companions are at risk of death; their friends will therefore 'commit' divine mercy — they make an urgent appeal to the God of heaven to save them. The word carries the idea of a determined action, a request that cannot be ignored.
H7359.origine: This Aramaic word is the form of the Hebrew רַחֲמִים (rahamim), 'compassion' or 'bowels of mercy'. The root first evokes the maternal womb, then by extension tenderness and pity. The transition from Hebrew to Aramaic shows that the book of Daniel, partly written in Aramaic, uses this vocabulary of divine mercy in a context of extreme crisis.
H7359.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 2:18. It is a critical moment: King Nebuchadnezzar has ordered the execution of all the wise men of Babylon, and Daniel risks perishing with them. His friends will then 'commit' the mercy of the God of heaven — that is, they will make a pressing supplication to Him. The context emphasizes that this approach is the only recourse in the face of a deadly threat.
H7359.portee: This word reminds us that prayer is not just a quiet conversation with God: it can be an urgent supplication, a cry from the heart in the face of danger. It also teaches that in extreme crises, one must seek divine mercy insistently and passionately, without resignation.

sens: unclean aquatic bird according to the law of Moses
voracious and scavenging bird
H7360.detail:
1. The cormorant is an aquatic bird that the Mosaic law classifies among unclean animals, prohibited for consumption. It appears in both biblical lists of forbidden birds, alongside the pelican and the swan (Leviticus 11:18 and Deuteronomy 14:17). These lists served to mark the boundaries of what was pure or impure in the daily life of the people of Israel.
2. The name itself evokes a bird of prey or carrion, which justifies its classification among unclean creatures: the cormorant lives in the waters, dives to catch fish, or feeds on carrion, behaviors that the Israelite was to reject as defiled. It is a formidable and solitary water predator.
H7360.origine: The Hebrew word רָחָם (rāḥām) literally designates this aquatic bird, but the Bible does not provide further details on its precise identification. It classifies it among unclean birds, those from which the people must refrain. The word belongs to the vocabulary of animals and creatures, a list that God gives to Moses to teach Israel to distinguish between the clean and the unclean.
H7360.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, in the parallel verses of Leviticus and Deuteronomy that enumerate the forbidden birds. These two legal lists are identical and serve as the foundation for the dietary law of the people of Israel. The cormorant is always mentioned alongside other aquatic or predatory birds, such as the pelican, the swan, or the grebe. No figurative use: it is always a practical and ritual classification.
H7360.portee: This word reminds the reader that the law of Moses did not simply separate the people by abstract rules, but by concrete daily actions: what one eats, what one refuses. The cormorant, visibly impure by its nature as a scavenging aquatic bird, illustrates how God wanted to teach Israel to discern between the holy and the profane in the most ordinary creatures.

sens: Who feels compassion, tenderness in the face of the suffering of others
Moved by the misfortunes of another, capable of sympathy
H7362.detail:
1. Compassionate describes someone who feels tenderness, natural compassion towards those who suffer. It is a heart inclination to share in another's pain and to want to help. In Lamentations 4:10, the prophet emphasizes the horror of the famine during the siege of Jerusalem: even women, naturally compassionate towards their children, resorted to cooking them to eat — so great was the misery that it surpassed all ordinary human feelings.

2. The word thus evokes an innate quality, a tenderness of heart that drives one to care for those who suffer. This natural compassion of mothers for their little ones is so strong that its violation reveals the abyss of catastrophe.
H7362.origine: The Hebrew word רַחֲמָנִי (rach.ma.ni) comes from the root רחם (racham), which means 'to have pity, to be merciful'. This root is related to רֶחֶם (rechem), the womb or maternal breast, as compassion is primarily that of a mother towards the child she has borne. The word describes one who possesses this natural capacity for tenderness and mercy.
H7362.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Lamentations 4:10. The prophet Jeremiah, contemplating the ruins of Jerusalem after the siege of 586 B.C., evokes the monstrous inversion of feelings: compassionate women had to commit the unthinkable. This unique usage shows how the text employs this term to amplify the horror — it is precisely because they are naturally tender that their act reveals the extremity of famine and disaster.
H7362.portee: This word reminds us that compassion is a deep and natural feeling, particularly in those who protect life. By pointing out this feeling in women, the text highlights how extreme suffering can invert our most basic values. For the Christian, it is a call to never forget how sin and its consequences devastate humanity, and to not remain indifferent to the misfortunes of others.

sens: To be physically shaken by a violent emotion
To be seized with weakness or fear in the face of something serious
H7363A.detail:
1. The verb describes a physical shaking of the body, like bones involuntarily quaking under the effect of intense emotion. In Jeremiah 23:9, the prophet says that all his bones 'tremble' when he contemplates the holiness of God and the weight of His words: it is an emotion that shakes the entire body, comparable to drunkenness.
2. More broadly, the word expresses a moral weakness or a deep disturbance in the face of something formidable. It is not a simple shiver: it is the effect of confronting what surpasses man and stirs him to the core.
H7363A.origine: The Hebrew verb רָחַף (rachaph) evokes the idea of losing firmness, becoming soft or unstable. The root suggests a loss of stability — the opposite of solidity and assurance. This trembling is involuntary: it manifests what stirs the soul from within.
H7363A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible (in Jeremiah 23:9). The prophet Jeremiah uses it to describe his state when he receives or proclaims the holy word of the Lord. It is not an ordinary fear, but a religious awe: it is the prophet's reaction to the gravity of what he must announce, especially when he denounces false prophets. The image of bones trembling reinforces the idea of a total shaking, down to the roots of the body.
H7363A.portee: This passage teaches that contact with the holiness of God and His words can stir the believer's heart to trembling. Jeremiah does not boast of his prophetic authority: he instead shows his human fragility in the face of the gravity of the message he bears. This reminds us that faith is not the absence of trouble, but a sincere reaction to the majesty of God.

sens: To move in a light and undulating flight above a place
To have an active and protective presence without landing
H7363B.detail:
1. The verb describes a flight movement characterized by undulations and lightness: the Spirit of God "hovered" over the waters during creation (Genesis 1:2), like a presence that glides and soars without stopping. It is the image of a force that moves in light flight, suspended, ready to act.
2. The word also evokes a protective and watchful presence: the eagle that "hovers over its young" (Deuteronomy 32:11) surrounds them with its attention, watches over them, and carries them on its wings. It is not simply flying; it is being present to protect and support.
H7363B.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of gentle and undulating movement. The image is that of a hovering presence: light, fluid, constantly in motion above something. This root belongs to a family of words describing delicate movements and gestures of protection.
H7363B.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis 1:2, it describes the Spirit of God moving over the primordial waters before the creation of the world — an image of creative power in action, present and active. In Deuteronomy 32:11, it portrays the eagle hovering over its young to protect and teach them — an image of vigilant love and protective care. In both cases, the word emphasizes a living, mobile, and benevolent presence.
H7363B.portee: This verb reveals that God is not distant or inactive, but present, attentive, and in motion for the work of creation and the protection of His people. Like the eagle that hovers over its young, God surrounds His own with His constant vigilance. It is a powerful image of divine providence: a presence that is both gentle and active, hovering over our lives to support us.

sens: To wash the body or a part of the body with water
To wash clothes or objects
To wash oneself, to perform ablutions
To be ritually purified by washing, to become ritually clean
Figuratively, to be acquitted, washed of an accusation
H7364.detail:
1. To pour water over the body or a part of the body to clean it: this is the material act of washing. In Genesis 18:4, Abraham offers his guests "a little water, to wash your feet," a gesture of hospitality towards dusty travelers. Naaman seeks the rivers of Damascus "to wash in them and be clean" (2 Kings 5:12).
2. To clean clothes or objects by immersing or rubbing them in water. In Leviticus 15:5-6, anyone who touches an unclean object must wash their clothes.
3. To clean oneself, particularly in the rituals of worship or purity. In Exodus 30:21, the priests "shall wash their hands and feet" at the basin, a daily ritual of purification before service.
4. To be ritually purified by a washing of water, according to the Law. In Leviticus 14:9, the healed leper "shall bathe his body in water" to be declared clean: the washing removes legal impurity.
5. Figuratively, to be acquitted or freed from guilt, as if the water removes the accusation. In Psalm 26:6, the psalmist says, "I will wash my hands in innocence," to affirm his righteousness before God.
H7364.origine: The Hebrew verb rachats means "to wash" or "to bathe," describing the action of water that purifies. The root evokes immersion or the passage of water over a surface. The word belongs to a family of ancient images of cleaning and purification, natural to a culture where water was precious and worship required rituals of purity. The washing of hands, feet, and the entire body is prevalent in the Old Testament as a sign of hygiene, respect, and conformity to God's laws.
H7364.emploi: The verb rachats appears 71 times in Biblical Hebrew, mainly in the legal books (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers) and in narratives. It primarily denotes the mundane act: washing the feet of a guest (Genesis 18:4, 19:2, 24:32), washing after a day (2 Samuel 11:2). But it takes on significant weight in worship: priests must wash their hands and feet before approaching the altar (Exodus 30:19-21), and those who become ritually unclean through contact with corpses or discharges must wash to regain purity (Leviticus 15 and 16). In Isaiah 1:16, the prophet calls for moral purification: "Wash yourselves, make yourselves clean." In the Psalms, washing becomes the image of innocence (Psalm 26:6) or of divine retribution (Psalm 58:11). The meaning progresses from the physical (removing dirt) to the ritual (regaining access to the sacred) to the spiritual (standing pure before God).
H7364.portee: This word shows that for Israel, physical purity was inseparable from the relationship with God: washing the body was not just an act of hygiene, but an act of submission to God's holiness. Ritual washing reminded that sin soils just as dirt soils, and that one must be purified to approach the Lord. For the Christian, Jesus fulfills and transforms these washings: the sacrifice of the cross purifies us internally, far more effectively than the water of the basin. The language of washing remains alive to express forgiveness and regeneration.

sens: To rely on someone or something, to count on their faithfulness or power
To place one's assurance in the Lord rather than in the things of the world
H7365.detail:
1. To trust means to rely on someone or something, being convinced that they will not abandon us. It is an inner act of the soul: one renounces relying on oneself or on men, and rests entirely on the one in whom one believes. In Daniel 3:28, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego trusted in their God: they risked their lives by refusing to worship the golden statue of the king of Babylon, certain that the Lord would protect them.
2. This trust is a voluntary commitment: one consciously places it in someone. It arises from the experience of the goodness and power of the one in whom one believes. For a believer, trusting in God means granting His word and providence greater authority than fear or appearances.
H7365.origine: The Hebrew verb רָחַץ (rachats) has a basic bodily image: to wash, to immerse — hence the idea of purifying or completely surrendering to something. Here, in its reflexive form (Hithpa'el), it literally means "to place oneself in trust in": one rests, one surrenders to the one in whom one trusts, like someone who lets themselves be carried by water. This verb expresses the idea of a complete abandonment of oneself.
H7365.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 3:28. It is a late narrative (Babylon), and this rare Hebrew word appears in a context of extreme religious courage. The three young Hebrews are praised for having "trusted" in God in the face of the death threat, refusing to bow to the king's power. The unique usage suggests that this term may have been chosen to emphasize the intensity of their surrender to divine will in a situation where everything seemed lost.
H7365.portee: This trust that the three young men placed in God despite the mortal danger reminds the believer that true strength does not come from worldly prudence or submission to human powers, but from the assurance that God is faithful. For those reading Daniel today, it is an invitation to place their trust in God even when human reason advises compromise.

sens: Action of washing, cleaning with water
Basin or container used for washing
H7366.detail:
1. Washing is the action of cleaning something with water. In the Psalms, the king says, "Moab is the basin where I wash" (Psalms 60:10; 108:10): he uses a poetic image to express his dominance over enemy countries, just as one freely uses everyday objects. Here, washing evokes not only physical cleaning but also mastery and possession.
2. The word also refers to the basin itself, the container intended for washing. When the psalmist declares, "Moab is the basin where I wash," he is not only speaking of the action but of the basin itself, transformed into an image of disdain: it is like saying, "Moab has become my object of service."
H7366.origine: The Hebrew word רַחַץ (rachats) comes from a root that means "to wash" or "to clean." It is related to the idea of purification and running or stagnant water. Washing was a daily and religious practice in Israel, attested in purification rites and ablutions. The word refers both to the action and sometimes to the basin or container used for this action.
H7366.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 60:10 and 108:10, two parallel passages from the same psalm (or composed from the same source). In both cases, the king of Israel uses the image of washing to symbolically express his absolute dominance over his neighbors: Moab becomes for him like a washing basin, a domestic object at his disposal. This poetic image transforms a daily act of hygiene into a declaration of political power. The context is one of a promise of victory over Israel's enemies.
H7366.portee: This passage shows us how the Bible uses images from daily life — here washing — to express spiritual and political realities. It reminds us that domination is not just a military matter, but of recognized and absolute sovereignty. For the believer, it is also an invitation to see how God uses simple and concrete images to help us understand profound truths about His authority and mastery over the world.

sens: place where animals come to drink
smooth and shiny aspect of teeth
H7367.detail:
1. A trough is a designated place where herds come to drink, that is, to drink water. In Song of Solomon 4:2 and 6:6, the image of teeth compared to sheep "coming up from the trough" evokes both purity (the sheep coming from the bath) and the shiny regularity of teeth.
2. Through this poetic comparison, the word also refers to the smooth, shiny, and well-aligned aspect of teeth, as if they had been washed and polished. This image praises the beauty of the smile: white, regular, and sparkling teeth, a symbol of youth and health.
H7367.origine: The Hebrew word rach.tsah comes from a root that expresses the idea of washing, cleaning. The trough is literally a place of washing and water. This same root is found in other Hebrew words related to ablution and purification, important concepts in the religious life of Israel.
H7367.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the Song of Solomon (4:2 and 6:6), in identical verses that describe the beloved's teeth. The usage is purely poetic and metaphorical: it is never used in the literal sense of a place where domestic animals drink. It is an image of beauty typical of the poetry of the Song, where the body of the beloved is described through comparisons with nature and the animal world.
H7367.portee: This image reminds us that the Bible speaks of beauty and love without hesitation. It also shows us how biblical poetry paints vivid and simple pictures to express admiration and affection. For those reading the Song, it is an invitation to see beauty in the concrete details of life and the body, and to celebrate them as a gift from God.

sens: To be or become far, distant, remote
To go far away, to depart
To put or send far away, to remove, to keep at a distance
To end, to withdraw, to make disappear
To distance morally or spiritually
To cease approaching, to withdraw
H7368.detail:
1. This word first describes the physical reality of distance: to be far, to become far. Hagar sat "a bowshot away" (Genesis 21:16), that is, at a distance from her child, far from him.
2. It also describes the action of going away, departing, withdrawing. The enemy troops of Gideon "distanced themselves" (Judges 18:22) by retreating from the battlefield.
3. The verb can also mean to send someone far away, to put at a distance. The Lord "distanced" the locusts from the land of Egypt (Exodus 8:24), driving them away.
4. In a broader sense, it means to remove, to take away, to make disappear: God can "distance" iniquity (Job 22:23), that is, to remove it, to banish it.
5. The word takes on a spiritual dimension when it speaks of straying from God's path: those who "distance themselves" from His law turn away from it (Psalms 119:150), they stray from obedience.
6. It can also express the action of keeping away, not approaching: God asks to distance oneself from falsehood (Exodus 23:7), not to come near it, to flee from it.
H7368.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the image of space that opens up between two things. It forms a family of words around distance and retreat: "far," "distant," "distance." The word can be used in the active voice (someone distances something) or passive voice (something distances itself, becomes far). It is a concrete word at its core, describing space and separation, before taking on spiritual meanings.
H7368.emploi: The verb "to distance" appears about 55 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms, Job, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. It is used first in a physical sense: walking at a distance, sitting far away, withdrawing (Genesis 21:16; Joshua 8:4). It also describes the action of God or a king who chases away, expels, ends something: God distances the locusts (Exodus 8:24), the peoples (Joel 2:20), or He distances anger (Psalms 103:12). In the Psalms, it takes on a supplicatory tone: the psalmist asks God not to distance Himself from him (Psalms 35:22), to be close in need. Among the wise (Job, Proverbs), it describes how to stray from sin: fleeing falsehood, distancing oneself from the adulterous woman (Proverbs 5:8). Isaiah uses it to describe how God pushes back boundaries and multiplies the people (Isaiah 26:15).
H7368.portee: This word invites the Christian to understand spiritual distance: it can be physical and legitimate (distancing oneself from evil, Proverbs 5:8), or it can be rupture and suffering (the psalmist who fears that God will distance Himself, Psalms 35:22). It reminds us that intimacy with God is not given: it requires not straying from Him, and it assumes that God Himself does not distance Himself. This word also speaks of God's purifying action, which drives away evil and clears the way for His people.

sens: To move away, to keep at a distance
To abandon, to turn away from someone or something
To separate, to withdraw
To become far away, distant
H7369.detail:
1. The word describes the physical or moral action of moving away, creating distance. In Psalms 73:27, "those who are distant from you" refers to those who voluntarily turn away from God, separating themselves through their conduct.
2. More broadly, it is the act of standing apart, abandoning a relationship or position. The image is of someone fleeing or turning their back.
3. On a spiritual level, it is to refuse closeness with God, to cease being faithful to Him. Those who "are distant" from God in the Psalms text are those who live in unfaithfulness.
H7369.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to be far," "to be distant." It evokes the image of a spatial or moral separation. The verb describes the action of creating this distance, of moving away or being rejected. The family of words revolves around the idea of absence, of breaking proximity.
H7369.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible according to recorded uses, in Psalms 73:27. It describes those who "are distant" from God, meaning those who abandon their relationship with Him. In this psalm context, the distancing is not accidental: it is a voluntary act of defection, unfaithfulness. The verse contrasts those who are distant with the psalmist who seeks to remain close to God ("but for me, drawing near to God is my happiness"). The use emphasizes the fatal consequence: those who are distant perish.
H7369.portee: This word invites the reader to be aware of the danger of distancing oneself from God. It reminds that the relationship with God requires proximity — an intimacy of heart and faithful life. To distance oneself is not neutral: it is a choice that leads to ruin. For the believer, this word calls to remain attached to God, not to drift far from His presence and will.

sens: To move continuously, with agitation and fluidity, like a liquid that boils or bubbles
To overflow, to surge with force and abundance
To express oneself with fervor and passion, speaking of words or thoughts
H7370.detail:
1. The word describes a constant and tumultuous movement: the image is of a liquid that boils, agitating without cease. It is a state of continuous flow, where something active manifests without rest. In Psalms 45:2, the psalmist says that words "bubble" in his heart — they are not fixed, they ferment, they surge from him in abundance.
2. The idea of overflowing: what bubbles tends to overflow, to spread. There is no restraint, but lush expression. The psalmist's heart is so full of words concerning the king that they naturally spring forth, like a source that flows continuously.
3. On an emotional and spiritual level, bubbling speaks of passion, of vivid and deep emotion. These are not cold or distant words: they come from the heart, animated by inner fervor. The context of the royal psalm shows sincere exaltation, a joyful effervescence.
H7370.origine: The Hebrew root רחש (ra-chash) evokes continuous movement, agitation, turmoil. It is related to the idea of flow, of incessant circulation. The word carries the sensory image of a substance that stirs, boils, or murmurs — one thinks of boiling water, of rustling wind. It is a very descriptive verb, which paints rather than states.
H7370.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 45:2. It is used poetically to describe the emotional and verbal state of the psalmist in the presence of his subject (the king). The context is that of composing a royal hymn: the poet confesses that his heart bubbles with words, so overflowing is his enthusiasm. It is a word of lyrical poetry, chosen for its expressive strength and vivid imagery.
H7370.portee: This word reminds us that true speech — that which comes from the heart, which is charged with conviction and passion — does not emerge from cold reflection, but from inner effervescence. For the believer, it invites seeking a faith that is not merely intellectual, but deep and overflowing, expressed with naturalness and sincerity. It is also an image of what happens when the heart is truly touched by the greatness of God or by His love: the words can no longer be restrained.

sens: Flat and wide tool used to separate grain from chaff
By extension, agricultural tool for sifting or cleaning
Image of what separates and purifies
H7371.detail:
1. The winnowing shovel is a flat and wide agricultural tool that is shaken to make the chaff (the husk of the grain) fly away while the heavier grain falls back down. In Isaiah 30:24, the prophet describes the grain processed "with the shovel and the winnowing fan," meaning completely cleaned and prepared for livestock feed.
2. More broadly, the shovel refers to any utensil used for sifting, winnowing, or cleaning the harvest. It is a humble but indispensable object in the work of the fields in ancient Israel.
3. In biblical language, the image of the winnowing shovel becomes an image of purification and separation: separating what is valuable (the grain) from what is useless (the chaff), which can evoke a divine judgment that separates the good from the bad.
H7371.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to sift" or "to pass through a sieve." It is related to the idea of passing something through a sieve or shovel to clean and sort it. It is a concrete word, describing a gesture of daily agricultural work in the Middle East.
H7371.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 30:24. It is used in a context describing the work of the fields: the prophet lists the food given to oxen and donkeys, and mentions the grain that will be "winnowed with the shovel and the winnowing fan." It is a concrete detail that shows the richness and abundance of the promised land after judgment.
H7371.portee: This word reminds us that simple agricultural work and the care taken to prepare food were at the heart of life in Israel. The image of the shovel separating grain from chaff also inspires reflection on divine judgment: God purifies His people as one purifies grain, removing what is barren or harmful.

sens: To have the quality of being soaked or imbued with water
State of that which retains moisture, particularly wood or fibers
Character of that which is not dry, that which has retained its water
H7372.detail: 1. The verb describes the state of something that has absorbed water or remains wet: it is not dry, it retains moisture. In Job 24:8, the poor who have no clothing to cover themselves are wet from the rain due to lack of shelter — the humidity has settled in them. 2. In the context of wood or fabrics, it is the natural state or resulting from water absorption: the fibers swell, the weight increases. It is the opposite of drying out. 3. The word can also evoke the absence of general dryness, an atmosphere or overall state saturated with humidity.
H7372.origine: The Hebrew verb רָטֵב (ratav) comes from a root that expresses the idea of absorbing water, of being soaked. The same root appears in agricultural and climatic contexts. The underlying image is that of water penetrating and filling spaces, transforming the texture and solidity of what it touches.
H7372.emploi: This verb is very rare in biblical Hebrew: it occurs only once in Job 24:8. It appears in a poetic description of extreme misery, where the poor lack protection against the elements and suffer from the humidity and cold of the night. The context shows a degraded physical state, associated with dispossession and suffering.
H7372.portee: This word invites the reader to feel concretely the condition of one who suffers: to be wet is to be struck by cold and discomfort, without recourse. It is a cry for compassion towards the abandoned and a reminder that God sees those who are crushed by injustice.

sens: State of freshness and vitality
Flourishing of the plant or tree
Vital force, youth
Manifested energy
H7373.detail: 1. This Hebrew word primarily describes the physical freshness of a well-living plant, saturated with sap: a "vigorous" wood is moist, juicy, full of life. 2. By extension, it evokes the flourishing of a healthy tree: in Job 8:16, it is this verdant freshness that allows the plant to generously extend its branches and bear fruit. 3. The word also applies to human youth, to that vital impulse that characterizes one who has not been crushed by misfortune. 4. Figuratively, it is the underlying power, the inner energy that manifests blessing and life.
H7373.origine: The Hebrew root rṭb means to be moist, soaked, fresh — the fundamental image is that of vital moisture running through the fibers of wood. It refers to the saps of living trees, the water that gives the plant its flexibility and growth strength. The word belongs to the same family as "ratan" and Arabic words denoting fruitful moisture.
H7373.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 8:16. It is used to describe the tree of the hypocrite that temporarily prospers: even deeply dried out, it retains a surface sheen of freshness. The context is that of the apparent prosperity of one who forgets God — an image that Bildad uses to say that nothing is enduring without the Lord.
H7373.portee: This word teaches us that true life — the vigor that lasts — comes from the inner moisture that only God can give. A prosperity that is merely surface freshness, like that of the hypocrite in Job, will dry up; only communion with God maintains the vital sap.

sens: Physical and mental trembling caused by sudden and intense fear
Panic that seizes a person or community in the face of danger
H7374.detail: 1. The word denotes a trembling, an agitation of the body and mind in the face of an overwhelming threat. It is a visceral reaction, a fear that shakes the entire being. In Jeremiah 49:24, fear seizes Damascus: the city trembles in terror at the approach of judgment, like a woman seized by the pains of childbirth. 2. It is also collective panic, that state where fear paralyzes an entire community. It prevents clear thinking and drives to flight. Damascus can only turn to flee, unable to resist or reflect.
H7374.origine: The Hebrew word derives from a root that expresses the idea of trembling and wavering. It first evokes a physical movement — that of the body shaken by fear — before describing the emotional state itself. It is not a simple worry, but a deep agitation that engages the whole body.
H7374.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 49:24, to describe the fear that seizes Damascus during its judgment. The prophetic context shows how a strong city can be reduced to trembling and flight by the word of God. Fear is presented as the natural effect of divine judgment: those who refuse to turn to God are seized by terror.
H7374.portee: This word reminds the reader that fear can seize us when we are confronted with a reality greater than our strength. For one who knows God, it shows the importance of taking refuge in Him rather than relying on one's own resources. Fear thus becomes a warning: it invites us not to resist the word of God, but to listen to it.

sens: To have the appearance or qualities of something new, vigorous, intact
H7375.detail: 1. The word evokes something that regains its original vigor, its primary strength — like a body that regains health and youth. In Job 33:25, Eliphaz describes the healing process: when a man escapes death by God's grace, his flesh "becomes softer than that of a child," it "returns to a fresh state" of youth. It is the image of physical and vital regeneration.
H7375.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of what is tender, moist, full of life — in contrast to what is dry, worn out, or dead. The word belongs to the family of terms describing youth, tenderness, and vigor. The Niphal form (passive or reflexive) emphasizes that this renewal is not an action one undertakes oneself, but a change that occurs in us, often through divine intervention.
H7375.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 33:25. In this poetic passage, Eliphaz speaks of the miraculous restoration of the body after a serious illness: the sick person's flesh "becomes fresh" like that of a child, symbolizing God's healing power and His ability to give new life to those who believe in Him.
H7375.portee: This word reminds us that divine restoration is not just a matter of spiritual forgiveness: it touches the whole person. When God heals, He restores vigor and youth. For the believer, this evokes God's power to renew, not only in this life but also in the hope of resurrection.

sens: To violently break something by striking or pressing it
To destroy, reduce to nothing
To kill by crushing, especially children and pregnant women during an invasion
H7376.detail: 1. The verb describes the action of breaking or pulverizing something with a brutal blow or violent force — as if one crushes pottery against the ground. In 2 Kings 8:12, Elisha speaks of the evils that Hazael will inflict on Israel: he will "crush" the little children of the Israelites. 2. The word extends to the sense of completely destroying, ruthlessly ruining. In Isaiah 13:16, during an invasion, children "will be crushed before the eyes" of their parents, an image of total destruction of a community. 3. The word takes on its full force in prophetic judgment texts: it denotes the violent murder of innocents — children, pregnant women — during wars and exiles. In Hosea 13:16 and Nahum 3:10, "to crush" is the extreme act of wartime cruelty, a symbol of inevitable divine punishment.
H7376.origine: The Hebrew root rāṭaš evokes the idea of a violent blow, of fragmentation. It belongs to the family of verbs of destructive action. The word is used in the Piel (intensive form) to express the voluntary and repeated action of crushing, and in the Pual for the passive result of being crushed. This root conveys the raw horror of judgment: no nuance, no escape.
H7376.emploi: The verb appears six times in the Old Testament, always in a context of divine judgment or war catastrophe. It is concentrated in the prophets of threat (Isaiah, Hosea, Nahum) and in the account of Elisha's prophecy (2 Kings 8:12). Each use reinforces the horror: the word always targets the most vulnerable — little children, pregnant women — and emphasizes that judgment affects not only the guilty but an entire generation. The Segond regularly translates "to crush" (three-quarters of the cases), but also sometimes "little" or "people" depending on the grammatical context.
H7376.portee: This brutal word forces the reader not to turn away from the real consequences of sin and divine judgment: punishment does not only strike abstract culprits, but destroys concrete lives, innocents. For the believer, it reminds us that rebellion against God is not a trivial act — it leads to visible ruin and undeniable suffering. It is a call to repentance that hides nothing of the gravity.

sens: water or water vapor contained in the air or in clouds
H7377.detail: 1. This word concretely refers to humidity, water dispersed in the atmosphere as vapor or droplets. In Job 37:11, it describes how God fills the clouds with humidity — the raw material of the rains that fertilize the earth.
H7377.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of watering, soaking. It is related to terms that describe water that quenches and gives life. Its unique use in the Bible underscores the importance of this fundamental process: the water from heaven that nourishes all living creatures.
H7377.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 37:11, where the character Elihu contemplates God's works in nature. He speaks of how God "fills the clouds with his humidity." This cosmic and contemplative context shows that the word refers to a divine process: the creation and distribution of water that sustains the world.
H7377.portee: This word reminds us of a simple yet profound truth: life on earth depends on the water that God sends from heaven. For the believer reading Job, it is an invitation to see in the most ordinary natural phenomena — rain, dew, clouds — signs of divine providence and care for His creatures.

sens: To enter into dispute, to quarrel with someone, exchange of sharp words
To engage in a lawsuit, to plead a case before the court
To address a reprimand, a criticism to someone
To defend a cause, to support it against an opponent
To complain, to make a claim against someone
H7378.detail:
1. To enter into dispute or to quarrel: this is the most direct and common meaning of the word, a verbal confrontation where people oppose each other with words. For example, the shepherds of Gerar "quarreled" with Isaac's shepherds over water (Genesis 26:20). It is also the meaning when Moses says that Israel "contended" against God at the waters of Meribah (Deuteronomy 33:8).
2. To engage in a lawsuit or plead: the word then evokes the action of suing someone in court, of supporting a cause before a tribunal. In Proverbs 23:11, it is written that the "avenger" of orphans "will defend their cause against you," meaning he will act in justice against those who oppress them.
3. To reprimand or criticize: this is the use of the verb to designate a solemn correction addressed to someone. Nehemiah "reprimanded the nobles and officials" who charged interest (Nehemiah 5:7).
4. To defend a cause, to support it: the word then takes on the meaning of protecting or pleading for someone or something against an opponent. Isaiah cries out: "He who justifies me is near: who will contend against me?" (Isaiah 50:8), meaning who will dare to accuse or oppose me?
5. To complain or claim: the word can also mean to formulate a complaint, to express a grievance. When Israel "contended" against Moses in the desert (Exodus 17:2), the people were complaining and demanding water.
H7378.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of standing against someone, opposing. It is close to the image of two adversaries facing each other in a verbal or legal struggle. This same root is found in other Hebrew words meaning "adversary" or "lawsuit." The word fundamentally expresses the idea of confrontation and opposition, whether by word, by justice, or by force.
H7378.emploi: This verb appears 59 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the historical books (Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Judges, Samuel), in the wisdom books (Job, Proverbs), and in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Micah). The context varies considerably: it can be a simple quarrel between shepherds (Genesis 26:20), a complaint from the people against Moses (Exodus 17:2), a legal confrontation (Proverbs 23:11), or an accusation against God Himself (Jeremiah 2:9). Very often, the word is used to describe conflicts with God: Israel "contends" against Him, and God "contends" against Israel to accuse them of their unfaithfulness. The meaning thus nuances from simple human conflict to solemn divine judgment.
H7378.portee: This word reminds the reader that every contention, every conflict or lawsuit is known and judged by God. When the Bible shows Israel "contending" against Moses or against God, it invites us to recognize God's authority and His will. Conversely, the promise that God "will defend the cause" of the weak (Proverbs 23:11) becomes a source of hope for those who are oppressed: God Himself will plead for them, even if no human does.

sens: Conflict, confrontation between two or more people
Verbal dispute, exchange of sharp words
Contradictory debate brought before a judge
Disagreement, discord that divides
Action of defending one's cause, one's right
H7379.detail:
1. A quarrel is primarily a physical or verbal conflict between people: Abram and Lot cannot live together because a quarrel breaks out between their shepherds (Genesis 13:7). It is direct opposition, often loud and visible.
2. It becomes a dispute when both parties exchange harsh or accusatory words, fueling tension and resentment — Proverbs 15:18 and 26:21 show that some people "seek" or "stir up" quarrels.
3. Presented before judges, it takes the form of a case to be decided: in court, two men appear with their quarrel to be judged, one acquitted and the other condemned (Deuteronomy 25:1).
4. It is also a disagreement that can last and cause harm: Hosea speaks of the quarrel that Israel has with God, a reproach that accumulates.
5. Finally, "to defend one's cause" means to plead for justice to be done — Jeremiah entrusts his cause to the Lord, asking Him to rescue him from his adversaries (Jeremiah 11:20).
H7379.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root that means to contend, dispute. It designates both the conflict itself and the act of pleading. In biblical Hebrew, riv encompasses everything from a simple disagreement between people to a judicial trial. It is a very concrete word: it describes what is seen and heard when two wills oppose each other.
H7379.emploi: This word appears about 60 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the wisdom books (Proverbs, Job) and the Psalms, but also in history (Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, Samuel). Proverbs makes it a recurring theme: quarrel is a evil to be avoided (Proverbs 17:1 prefers calm over chaos), a contagious disease (it spreads like fire), and often it arises from foolishness. In the Psalms and among the prophets, defending one's cause becomes a prayer addressed to God: when a man is innocent and oppressed, he asks God to plead for him, for God alone is the just judge (Psalms 35:23).
H7379.portee: This word reminds Christians that quarrel is a reality to be faced: it arises from pride, resentment, and the refusal to forgive. Proverbs invites us to flee from it rather than to nourish it. But it also teaches that God is not indifferent to injustices: He is a judge, He hears the cause of those who suffer, and the believer can entrust his defense to Him rather than consuming himself in complaints.

sens: Man mentioned during the time of the united monarchy
Father of Ittai the Benjamite from Gibeah
Father of one of King David's elite warriors
H7380.detail: Ribai is a man living during the time of the united monarchy of Israel. He appears in the list of King David's most valiant warriors, known as the "Thirty" (2 Samuel 23:29 and 1 Chronicles 11:31). Ribai is best known as the father of Ittai, a Benjamite warrior from Gibeah, who himself is among these renowned warriors of King David.
H7380.origine: The name Ribai means "who contends with God" or "he who pleads with God," formed from the Hebrew root "rib" (to contend, dispute, plead) and the divine suffix "ja" (God). It is a theophoric name, common in Israel, expressing a relationship of intercession or justice before God.
H7380.emploi: Ribai is mentioned twice in the Bible, only in the list of the Thirty warriors of King David: in 2 Samuel 23:29 and in 1 Chronicles 11:31. These two parallel passages refer to the same man and report the same information: Ribai is the father of the warrior Ittai, a Benjamite from Gibeah who distinguished himself in the service of the king. This presence in the royal lists shows that his family enjoyed a certain military and social importance.

sens: Perfume or aroma that emanates from something, what is sensed by the nose
Pleasant, sweet, attractive scent
For the priest: the burnt offering whose smoke ascended to God
Image of what pleases God and receives His approval
H7381.detail:
1. Odor is simply what is perceived by the sense of smell when something exudes a scent. It is concrete and natural: in Song of Solomon 4:11, the odor of the beloved's garments is compared to that of Lebanon, a subtle perfume that enchants.

2. An odor can be pleasant and attract the one who smells it. Noah offers a sacrifice and the Lord "smelled a pleasing odor" (Genesis 8:21): the act of devotion ascended to God like a true scent, touching His heart.

3. In the worship of the Lord, "odor" refers to the burnt offering or the sacrifice consumed by fire. When the Levitical laws prescribe a "gift of a pleasing odor to the Lord" (Leviticus 2:9), they speak of what burns on the altar: the fat that rises in smoke, visible and perceptible, offered to the Lord.

4. Spiritually, this odor becomes the symbol of divine acceptance and communion with God. It is as if the sacrifice, rising in smoke, finds grace in the eyes of the Most High. The sacrifices offered "of a pleasing odor" testify that God accepts the heart of the faithful.
H7381.origine: The Hebrew word רֵיחַ (reïach) comes from a root that expresses the idea of smelling or breathing. Its equivalent in Aramaic has the same meaning. It is a basic word, rooted in sensory experience: odor is what passes through the nose and marks the soul. In the Bible, this word takes on theological depth by being applied to sacrifice: the odor becomes the vehicle of prayer and offering, what ascends to God in a visible and concrete manner.
H7381.emploi: The word appears 55 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated mainly in the sacrificial laws of Leviticus and Numbers. Its primary meaning remains sensory: Isaac recognizes his son by the "odor" of his garments (Genesis 27:27), and the Song uses "odor" to evoke the alluring beauty of the beloved (Song of Solomon 4:11). But the cultic context dominates: dozens of passages speak of "a pleasing odor" or "an odor of rest" (literally), characterizing the sacrifices offered at the altar. This technical term does not refer to a simple perfume: it means that the sacrifice, burned, acts as a rising prayer, which God receives and which appeases His anger. The nuance is subtle but decisive: the odor is no longer biological but liturgical and spiritual.
H7381.portee: This word teaches the believer that God is neither distant nor indifferent: He "smells" our offerings and acts of devotion. The notion of a pleasing odor reveals that God accepts the contrite and sincere heart of the one who offers themselves to Him. It is an invitation to present our lives not as formalities, but as living sacrifices that ascend to the Most High and find grace in His eyes.

sens: Olfactory sensation, perfume or stench that emanates from something
Physical trace of an action or presence, what remains after an event
H7382.detail:
1. Odor is what the nose perceives: a pleasant perfume or an unpleasant scent that emanates from an object or substance. In Daniel 3:27, it is the "odor of fire" — this trace of fire that should have marked the clothes and bodies of the three young men thrown into the fiery furnace. But the text states that this odor did not reach them, showing that the fire left no mark on them.
2. Odor can also refer more broadly to what remains of something after an event — the trace or imprint left behind. To say that the odor of fire did not reach them means that no sign of the fire remained on them: not a burn, not a singed hair, not even the scent of smoke.
H7382.origine: This Aramaic word comes from a Hebrew root rich in imagery: the idea of smelling, of breathing. The Hebrew word רֵיחַ (re'ach, H7381) also means "aroma" or "odor," and denotes everything that emanates from something and is captured by the nose. It is a concrete word, linked to the immediate sensation of the body.
H7382.emploi: The Aramaic word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 3:27. The book of Daniel is partially written in Aramaic, the language spoken in Babylon during the time of Nebuchadnezzar. This passage recounts the miracle of the three young Hebrews in the fiery furnace: the fire should have consumed them, but they emerge unharmed. The absence of the "odor of fire" on them is one of the supernatural proofs of the miracle — not even the odor had touched them.
H7382.portee: This detail of the "odor of fire" that did not reach them shows that the miracle is total and leaves no trace: God completely protects those who remain faithful to Him, even in the smallest details. It is an invitation to absolute trust in His power and goodness.

sens: Grain or cereal that has been crushed and ground
Food ground or reduced to fragments for consumption
H7383.detail:
1. The word refers to a grain or cereal that has been reduced to fragments, usually by grinding. In 2 Samuel 17:19, a woman spreads crushed grain over the opening of a well to conceal the hiding place of the messengers; this crushed grain could resemble dust or ordinary debris, serving as camouflage.
2. The word also applies to the result of grinding grains in a mortar, as an image of a repeated and futile action. In Proverbs 27:22, even if you were to grind the fool in a mortar "among the grains," his folly would remain attached to him — a telling comparison: all the grinding in the world would not change his nature.
H7383.origine: The Hebrew word ripah comes from a root that evokes grinding or crushing. Its exact etymology remains uncertain, but its meaning clearly refers to grains or cereals that have undergone mechanical transformation (grinding, milling). It is an infrequent word in the Bible, limited to these two distinct contexts.
H7383.emploi: The word ripah appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in the singular with the article or in direct construction. It appears once in 2 Samuel 17:19, where it serves a concrete purpose of camouflage, and once in Proverbs 27:22, where it enriches a moral comparison. In both cases, the image of crushed grain illustrates either an action masking a hidden reality or the ineffectiveness of repetition against a person's deep nature.
H7383.portee: This word reminds us that visible gestures and repeated efforts do not always change what is at the heart. In Proverbs, it underscores a spiritual truth: no external correction can transform the fool if he refuses wisdom. It is a lesson on the limits of human constraint in the face of pride and willful blindness.

sens: Son of Gomer, grandson of Japheth, according to the genealogy of the peoples
H7384A.detail: 1. Diphat is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogical list of the descendants of Noah. He is presented as the son of Gomer (who is himself the son of Japheth) and the brother of Ashkenaz and Togarmah (1 Chronicles 1:6). These genealogies reflect the distribution of ancient peoples known to the Israelites.
H7384A.origine: The name Diphat means "spoken" or "pronounced" in Hebrew. It is also found in the form Riphath (רִיפַת) in other textual traditions. Like many names in Genesis 10, it likely designates a people or region rather than an isolated individual, following the biblical convention where eponymous ancestors give their name to their descendants.
H7384A.emploi: Diphat appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 1:6. He is listed in the table of nations, a genealogical list that enumerates the peoples descended from Noah after the flood. This same character is called "Riphath" in Genesis 10:3, the first mention being. These two names designate the same ancestor; the orthographic variation reflects different textual traditions.

sens: son of Gomer and brother of Ashkenaz and Togarmah, a figure in the patriarchal genealogy
H7384B.detail: Riphat is one of the three sons listed of Gomer, himself a son of Japheth, in the table of nations in chapter 10 of Genesis (Genesis 10:3). He appears only once in the Bible as a link in a genealogy that enumerates the peoples of the ancient world and their origins. His name belongs to the category of founding ancestors whose descendants would have populated certain regions, according to the account of the dispersion after the flood.
H7384B.origine: The name Riphat means "spoken" or "who speaks." It is part of the genealogy of Japheth, one of the three sons of Noah. Ancient Jewish and Christian lexicographers often associated these names from Genesis 10 with historical peoples, although their precise identification remains debated among scholars. Riphat could refer to a people or a region in the Caucasus or ancient Asia Minor, but the biblical texts do not specify further.
H7384B.emploi: Riphat is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 10:3, in the enumeration of the descendants of Gomer. He is among the ancestors of the nations that, according to Genesis, dispersed after the flood. Alongside his brothers Ashkenaz and Togarmah, he represents a branch of the descendants of Japheth, one of the three major branches of humanity after Noah according to the biblical account.

sens: That which is devoid of content, emptied
That which produces no result, no fruit
That which is false, deceitful, unfounded
That which is futile, devoid of value or meaning
H7385.detail:
1. The word first describes what is empty, hollow, without real substance — the opposite of full and solid. When one sows in vain (Leviticus 26:16), one spreads seed on soil that will not hold it, that will not nourish it.
2. It characterizes any effort that leads nowhere, any work without effect: the fallen walls of Babylon signify that the nations "have worked in vain" (Jeremiah 51:58), meaning that their labor disappears, annihilated.
3. The word also designates what deceives, what cannot be trusted — false gods, false hopes. To love "vanity" (Psalms 4:3) means to cling to lies, to pursue dreams.
4. More broadly, it qualifies what is hollow in meaning, futile, without true value: the Egyptian "nothingness" (Isaiah 30:7) is a help that is worth nothing, that evaporates like noise.
H7385.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that first evokes emptiness, absence — that which has nothing inside. It is found in expressions describing nothingness, the void, that which flows or dissipates. The image is that of vanity: that which appears but does not last, that which promises but holds nothing.
H7385.emploi: This word appears about a dozen times in the Old Testament, especially among the prophets and in the Psalms. It first qualifies sterile effort: to sow in vain, to work in vain, to bear in vain (Isaiah 49:4, 65:23; Jeremiah 51:58). It then describes false objects of trust: idols, hollow ideas, powerless alliances. Isaiah 30:7 uses it for Egypt, a deceptive promise. The word can also qualify what causes sterile worry, a pain without foundation (Job 39:19). It is a word of the biblical spiritual decalogue: where vanity reigns, God is not.
H7385.portee: This word reminds the believer of the distinction between what is true and what is hollow, between the stable work of God and human endeavors that rely only on themselves. Understanding what is "vain" helps to reject false promises, efforts separated from God, and to anchor one's trust in what bears true fruit. It is an invitation to look at realities clearly.

sens: That which contains nothing, without matter
That which lacks substance or value
That which is hollow, without foundation
That which is futile, without profit
H7386.detail:
1. Empty first means the physical absence of content: the pit in Genesis 37:24 contains no water — it is completely empty. It is the state of a container that holds nothing.

2. The word then glides towards the absence of weight or value: the "men of nothing" in 2 Samuel 6:20 and 2 Chronicles 13:7 are despicable people, of no social or moral importance, literally "empty" of dignity.

3. In a more ethical sense, empty designates what is vain, hollow, without solid foundation. To pursue "vain" things (Proverbs 12:11) means to chase after dreams that will never nourish, projects without substance or blessing.

4. Finally, empty applies to that which is without profit or devoid of meaning: the tax in Nehemiah 5:13 that has no weight or validity is empty of binding force.
H7386.origine: The Hebrew word rēq comes from a root that means "to be hollow" or "to flow out." It evokes the image of a container that empties, of a liquid that flows out. The usage gradually extends from physical emptiness to moral emptiness: that which has nothing inside is worth nothing. It is a very concrete word at its source, but it quickly acquires a metaphorical dimension in biblical thought.
H7386.emploi: This word appears 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly to speak of empty objects (a pit, walls) or morally hollow people — "men of nothing" who are despicable or useless. It also describes vain enterprises or words: in Proverbs, to pursue vain things is to labor for nothing, without harvest. The word progresses from a very material sense to a spiritual and ethical sense: the absence of content becomes absence of value, the absence of filling becomes absence of meaning.
H7386.portee: For the believer, this word teaches the discernment between what truly nourishes and what leaves one dry. To pursue money, worldly honors, or pleasures without God is to cultivate emptiness. Conversely, a life founded on God and His word, even modest, is never in vain. It is a call not to waste one's life on hollow dreams that never satisfy.

sens: Without anything, hands or arms devoid of what one was carrying or possessing
Without having received what one expected, without benefit
Without result, without effect, in pure loss
Uselessly, without valid reason
H7387.detail:
1. The primary sense is concrete: when a person leaves or returns "empty," they have nothing with them. Ruth says: "the Lord has brought me back empty" (Ruth 1:21), she who was rich and returns stripped of everything. Laban would have sent Jacob "away empty" (Genesis 31:42), meaning without leaving him anything.
2. The idea expands to one who is deprived of what they should receive: God commands not to send away an emancipated slave or a poor person "empty" (Deuteronomy 15:13, Job 22:9), but to give them something to depart with dignity.
3. The word also designates total ineffectiveness: "the word that I speak shall not return to me empty" (Isaiah 55:11), it does not return without having made its effect. A prayer, a project, an ark of God sent back without an offering: all this would be "empty" of result.
4. In contexts where the uselessness or absurdity is emphasized: a warrior whose sword returns "empty" has accomplished nothing (2 Samuel 1:22).
H7387.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes emptiness, nothingness, absence. It first describes a physical state (hands, arms, a container devoid of content), then applies to any form of dispossession or ineffectiveness. It is a simple and expressive word from the concrete vocabulary of pastoral and domestic life.
H7387.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the Old Testament, especially in historical and wisdom books. It describes concrete situations: Jacob and Ruth leave or return empty (Genesis, Ruth); the Law requires not to send away the slave or the poor empty (Deuteronomy, Job). God also uses the word: His word does not return empty (Isaiah 55:11), it accomplishes what it was sent for. The common idea in all these uses is that of absence or lack: absence of goods, absence of effect, absence of blessing.
H7387.portee: This word reminds the reader that God does not condemn to poverty, but asks that we help others to depart with dignity. Ruth returns empty, but Boaz lifts her up and fills her. The word of God never returns empty: it always accomplishes what it promises, which is a source of trust for the believer. It is also a call to seek real effectiveness and lasting effect in one’s actions and prayers, rather than mere appearance.

sens: Viscous liquid produced by the mouth
Tasteless and flavorless substance
H7388.detail:
1. Saliva is the liquid that the mouth naturally produces: it is a mucus or drool. In 1 Samuel 21:13, David feigns madness by letting his saliva run down his beard to deceive King Achish — an act considered disgusting and degrading, a sign of mental alienation.
2. The Hebrew word also designates a viscous, odorless, and tasteless substance. In Job 6:6, it refers to the white of an egg, which is white, slippery, and tasteless: Job compares it to his food of the unfortunate, which neither nourishes nor satisfies.
H7388.origine: The Hebrew word rir (רִיר) literally refers to anything that flows or spills from the mouth — a viscous humor. It evokes the idea of something liquid and slimy. The same root word reappears in other images of substances that flow or spread, conveying what comes out of the body involuntarily or disgustingly.
H7388.emploi: This word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In 1 Samuel 21:13, it describes the saliva that David deliberately lets flow to simulate madness before a foreign king — an act of humiliation that is both played and effective. In Job 6:6, it designates the egg white, a white and inert mucus, to symbolize tasteless and frustrating food. In both cases, the term emphasizes the disgusting, bland, or repulsive nature of what flows or is offered to the palate.
H7388.portee: This word reminds us that disgust and repulsion are present in Scripture not to revolt us, but to show us the humiliation that a faithful person can endure (David before a king) and the spiritual hunger that leaves the soul empty and unfed (Job). It is an invitation to discern what truly nourishes.

sens: State of lack of material resources, indigence
Lack, insufficiency of what is necessary for life
Consequence of indiscipline and rejection of correction
Situation of fragility and powerlessness in the face of difficulties
H7389A.detail:
1. Poverty primarily refers to the absence of wealth, the state of a person who lacks material goods. While the rich are entrenched in a fortress of security, the poor remain vulnerable (Proverbs 10:15).
2. It is also a sudden lack: poverty arises like a thief or like a man armed, imposing itself without warning on one who has not been careful (Proverbs 6:11). It is a famine, a deprivation.
3. In wisdom literature, poverty is never simply an unfortunate accident: it becomes the lot of the lazy, of those who refuse discipline and reject correction (Proverbs 13:18).
4. Finally, it expresses powerlessness: it is the ruin that destroys the miserable, leaving them defenseless. That is why the wise man asks God for neither riches nor poverty, but simply daily bread (Proverbs 30:8).
H7389A.origine: The Hebrew word resh comes from a root that evokes what is broken, reduced, diminished. It belongs to the vocabulary of biblical wisdom, particularly among the sages of the Old Testament, to describe the state of one who has lost or never had the means to live decently. The word paints less a simple economic calculation than a condition of subjugation and fragility.
H7389A.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the Bible, exclusively in the book of Proverbs, the quintessential work of wisdom. The usages are therefore concentrated in moral and practical teaching: poverty is presented not as a fatality, but often as the result of poor choices (laziness in Proverbs 6:11 and 24:34, rejection of correction in Proverbs 13:18). It opposes wealth not only on a material level but also in terms of security and honor (Proverbs 10:15). Only once does the wise man express his wish to escape poverty, recognizing that it hinders inner freedom and obedience to God (Proverbs 30:8).
H7389A.portee: This word reminds the believer that the Bible does not see poverty as a mere passive misfortune, but often as the result of choices: indiscipline, laziness, and rejection of wisdom produce indigence. It thus invites personal responsibility. But it is never an absolute moral judgment: the wise man prays for neither riches nor poverty, recognizing that both can distance one from faithful service to God. It is an invitation to balance and dependence on God for what is necessary.

sens: State of one who lacks the necessities, who has no goods
Absence of resources, economic misery
State of destitution and material suffering
H7389B.detail:
1. Poverty primarily refers to the concrete lack of goods and resources: one who is poor does not have what is needed to live with dignity. In Proverbs 28:19, poverty is presented as the consequence of pursuing "vain things" instead of working: one who does not cultivate his field ultimately experiences it.
2. The word also evokes the state of misfortune and suffering that accompanies this material lack. In Proverbs 31:7, the unfortunate is advised to drink to forget his poverty and no longer remember his pains: poverty is linked to sorrow, grief, and the distress of one who suffers.
H7389B.origine: The Hebrew word rish comes from a root that expresses the idea of lack and destitution. It is a spelling variant of resh (רֵישׁ), both designating poverty. In biblical Hebrew, this word and its relatives express the absence of what is necessary for life.
H7389B.emploi: The word poverty (rish) appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in Proverbs. In these two passages, it designates a negative social and material condition, either as a consequence of idleness and lack of work (Proverbs 28:19) or a state of misery one wishes to forget (Proverbs 31:7). Biblical wisdom thus links poverty to the choices of those who endure it: it can be the fruit of negligence or vice.
H7389B.portee: Poverty is an important theme in biblical wisdom: it shows that choices and effort have concrete consequences in material life. The Christian is invited not to pursue illusions but to work honestly; he is also called to empathize with those who suffer from lack and misery, recognizing that poverty is a form of pain that can only be forgotten by seeking help from above.

sens: Soft, delicate, fragile to the touch
Young or inexperienced, physically weak
Lacking moral strength, timid, fearful
Gentle, kind in speech
H7390.detail:
1. The word primarily describes what is soft and delicate: the tender flesh of an animal (Genesis 18:7: Abraham takes "a tender and good calf"), or very young children who are still fragile (Genesis 33:13: the children are "delicate" and weary, Jacob fears to tire them).
2. It extends to youth and inexperience: Solomon is "of a weak age" (1 Chronicles 29:1), meaning very young to accomplish the great task of building the temple.
3. Morally and militarily, it denotes weakness of heart, fear: a "delicate" man who has lived in luxury will lack courage in battle (Deuteronomy 28:54), which is why tender-hearted men are sent away from the army (Deuteronomy 20:8).
4. In speech, the word qualifies kind gentleness: a "gentle" voice calms better than violence (Proverbs 15:1: "a gentle answer turns away wrath"), and gentle words can accomplish great things (Proverbs 25:15: "by gentleness one can sway the mighty").
H7390.origine: The Hebrew word rakh (רַךְ) comes from a root that evokes everything that is soft, flexible, yielding to pressure — the image of flesh that has not yet hardened, of a substance that sinks under the finger. Its derivatives in Hebrew retain this notion of suppleness or softness. In the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, it often translates the Greek word "apalos" (soft) and contrasts with what is hard, resistant, or mature.
H7390.emploi: This word appears sixteen times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily to describe physical fragility or inexperience (Genesis, 1 Chronicles) and moral weakness in the Law (Deuteronomy). The wisdom books use it for the gentleness of words (Proverbs, Job). David uses it regarding his royal weakness in the face of the sons of Zeruiah (2 Samuel 3:39). The word thus shifts between two realms: that of the biological (the young, the frail) and that of the moral (the gentle, the timid, the kind) — the two images ultimately converge, as what lacks physical strength often also lacks moral firmness.
H7390.portee: This word teaches an important wisdom: tenderness is not a shame, but it does not exempt one from growing. The Bible acknowledges that some are born fragile, young, or fearful — like Solomon at the time of his appointment. It also invites us to cultivate the tenderness of heart and speech as a spiritual strength, not as a weakness. Gentle responses and tender words often accomplish what violence cannot. Finally, it warns us: one should not remain tender indefinitely, but grow and strengthen one's heart to serve with courage.

sens: State of one who leads a life of comfort and delicacy, without effort or deprivation
Gentleness and refinement in demeanor or habits
H7391.detail:
1. The word denotes a cushy life, the habit of enjoying comfort and ease. The woman mentioned in Deuteronomy 28:56 grew up surrounded by comforts, so accustomed to well-being that she cannot endure hardships: she has become incapable of bearing the harshness of siege times, to the point that she will struggle even to walk on bare ground.
2. It also refers to the delicate and graceful demeanor of one who has not known physical fatigue. The same verse speaks of her delicacy, her refusal to "set the sole of her foot on the ground": an image of luxury and refinement in her habits.
H7391.origine: The Hebrew word rokh comes from a root that suggests the idea of softness and lack of firmness. It denotes the absence of hardness, the tendency to seek comfort and ease. It is a rare word in the Bible, used primarily to describe a social condition of wealth and material well-being.
H7391.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Deuteronomy 28:56. It is part of the description of the punishments that God will send upon Israel if His people disobey Him. Even the most delicate women, protected and nourished in abundance, will be reduced to such an extreme that they will forget their refinements and habits of comfort. The context is that of siege: famine and terror will erase even among the softest any filial or marital pity. The use of the word emphasizes the contrast between the sweetness of their past life and the horror they will have to face.
H7391.portee: This word reminds us that material comfort and the absence of difficulties do not guarantee strength of character or fidelity to essential values. The softness of a life too easy can render us incapable of persevering in the face of trials. For the believer, it is an invitation to seek spiritual strength rather than mere bodily well-being.

sens: To ride an animal and go upon it
To go on horseback or on another mount
To place someone on a mount
To ride into battle or in procession
Figuratively, to dominate or to soar (for divinity or a power)
H7392.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: to put one's foot on an animal and remain seated to move. Rebekah and her maidens "mounted" on the camels (Genesis 24:61): they climbed onto these beasts and departed with them. It is the simple act of mounting a horse, donkey, or camel.

2. To be a rider, that is, to go mounted on one's beast. The thirty sons of Jair "mounted" on thirty donkeys (Judges 10:4): this was their way of moving and showing themselves. The word can also refer to the rider himself — "rider" in the sense of one who mounts.

3. To place someone in the saddle, to lift him onto a mount to honor or transport him. They "made Solomon mount" on King David's mule (1 Kings 1:38), an act of enthronement: the royal officers lifted him and set him in the saddle to lead him to his coronation.

4. In war narratives, riding becomes combat and charge. Soldiers "mounted on horses" (Jeremiah 50:42) are the battle cavalry, armed and threatening — an image of military power.

5. In poetic biblical language, particularly for God: "He mounted on a cherub" (Psalms 18:11). Here, to mount does not describe a mere movement, but the majestic act of dominating, soaring, reigning. It is an image of sovereignty and divine glory.
H7392.origine: The Hebrew verb רָכַב (rakhav) comes from a root that denotes the action of riding, with the idea of rising up on something and remaining established on it. The noun רֹכֵב (rokhèv), "rider," derives directly from it — one who mounts. Other forms of the same root give words for "mount," "chariot," "cavalry." The basic image is that of movement and control: to mount is to take place above one's beast and direct it.
H7392.emploi: The verb "to mount" appears 75 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, mainly in narratives and poetry. From Genesis to Judges: one mounts a camel, donkey, or horse to travel (Genesis 24:61, Exodus 4:20) or to fight (Judges 5:10). From 1 Samuel to 2 Kings: the verb enriches with royal nuances — one "makes a king mount" in the saddle (1 Kings 1:38) — and military nuances — war cavalry, battle chariots.
