The Psalms and the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel) use "to mount" in a figurative sense: God "mounts" on a cherub (Psalms 18:11), He rides on the clouds (Isaiah 19:1), an image of divine domination. Zechariah 9:9, where the Messiah "mounts" on a donkey (alluding to the humble king), shows the symbolic charge of the verb. Everywhere, the idea is one of possession or majestic movement.
H7392.portee: This word reveals how the Bible views the relationship between the one who mounts and what he mounts: a relationship of mastery, but also of dependence — one needs their mount to go far. When the Psalms say that God "mounts on a cherub" or "rides on the wings of the wind," they express His unmatched sovereignty, His incomparable power. For the reader, "to mount" becomes an invitation to grasp that true power consists in being firmly established, to dominate one's circumstances — just as God dominates the elements. It is also a word that unites the everyday (traveling, fighting) and the divine (the glory of God).

sens: War or transport vehicle drawn by horses, mounted on wheels.
A group of horses and warriors forming a military unit.
The riders, the warriors mounted on a chariot or on horseback.
By extension, military power, the strength of a nation.
H7393G.detail:
1. A chariot is a war or ceremonial vehicle, drawn by horses and mounted on wheels. It is the means of transport for kings and high-ranking warriors in Israel and neighboring empires. Pharaoh pursues the Israelites "with his chariots" (Exodus 14:6), and Solomon possesses many as a sign of his wealth and power (1 Kings 10:26).

2. The word also designates a complete military formation: the horses, the chariot itself, and the warriors who drive or follow it. Thus, Judah could not drive out certain enemies "because they had iron chariots" (Judges 1:19) — it is an organized force.

3. By metonymy, the word "chariot" can also refer to the riders themselves, those who ride on horseback or in the chariot. When it is said that a king had "a thousand chariots" (2 Chronicles 1:14), it actually refers to the warriors and their equipment.

4. The chariot also symbolizes military power and the dominance of a people. To possess chariots is to have the advantage in war; to be without them is to be vulnerable to a better-equipped enemy.
H7393G.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "mounting" or "riding." The chariot itself is an object mounted on wheels, hence the image: it is what one rides upon. The Hebrews borrowed this vocabulary from their neighbors, notably the Egyptians and Hittites, who mastered the technology of the war chariot — a vehicle unknown or little known in Canaan before contact with these powers.
H7393G.emploi: The word appears 101 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and in war narratives. It first refers to Pharaoh's chariot (Exodus 14-15), then to the chariots of the kings of Canaan and Israel. Gradually, its meaning broadens: the word designates not only the material vehicle but also the riders or the entire military force. By the end of the 1st millennium B.C., when chariots lose military importance, the word can simply mean "cavalry" or "troop of riders." Finally, it takes on a symbolic value: Elijah is taken up "in a chariot of fire" (2 Kings 2:11), an image of divine power.
H7393G.portee: The chariot reminds the reader that victory in the Bible does not depend on military or technological power. Israel is often weaker in chariots than its enemies, but the Lord gives it victory (Psalms 20:8). This teaches Christians that trust in God takes precedence over trust in the means of the world.

sens: Circular stone used for grinding grains
Upper part of a mill (the one that turns on the lower stone)
Improvised weapon thrown from above
H7393H.detail:
1. A millstone is a heavy round stone, generally used in pairs: one fixed (the lower stone) and the other that turns on top (the upper stone) to grind grains into flour. It is an essential household tool for daily life in the ancient East.

2. The upper millstone, which "rides" on the lower millstone and is turned, is particularly important: Deuteronomy 24:6 prohibits it as a pledge, for depriving a family of its mill means taking away their means of livelihood — grains remain useless without it.

3. Its solidity and weight make it a fearsome weapon when thrown from the top of a wall. During the siege of Thebez, a woman throws a piece on Abimelech, crushing his skull (Judges 9:53; 2 Samuel 11:21): it is the very image of unexpected and deadly judgment.
H7393H.origine: The Hebrew word rekhev is related to the root rkb, which means "to mount, to ride." The upper millstone "rides" or "mounts" on the lower one — hence the name. In its primary sense, rekhev actually designates a harness, a chariot, or a rider (one who rides), but it takes on the specialized meaning of upper millstone here, probably by analogy: like a rider on his mount.
H7393H.emploi: The word appears three times in the Bible, always in the singular and always to designate a millstone. Deuteronomy 24:6 uses it in the literal sense: it is a necessity that cannot be seized as a pledge without depriving a family of the right to live. Judges 9:53 and 2 Samuel 11:21 report the same event: a woman throws a millstone from the top of the wall onto an assailant — here the word designates both the household object and the improvised weapon. In all cases, it is the image of a heavy, immobile, and indispensable stone, or one that has become an instrument of death.
H7393H.portee: These three uses draw a moral lesson. The millstone first symbolizes what allows one to live: feeding one's family. The Bible protects it by law, recognizing that certain goods are inviolable because they guarantee the life of the poor. Then the same millstone becomes a vengeful weapon in the hands of a woman: God uses the simplest and most unexpected means to overthrow the tyrant. It is an invitation to respect the dignity of the poor and to fear the judgment of God.

sens: Military chief during the time of Ish-Bosheth, son of Rimmon of Beeroth
Conspirator who assassinated Ish-Bosheth with his brother Baana
H7394G.detail: Recab is one of the two captains who served Ish-Bosheth, the son of Saul. With his brother Baana, he first appears as a military officer in the service of the king (2 Samuel 4:2). These two men are presented as sons of Rimmon of Beeroth, from a Benjaminite family. Recab and Baana conspired together to assassinate their king: they entered his house at noon during his nap and killed him by striking him in the belly (2 Samuel 4:5-6). After the crime, they fled, but David, who had just received news of Ish-Bosheth's death, sharply rebuked them for this act, which he considered a heinous murder, even though technically this act might have seemed political: David had Recab and Baana executed for shedding the innocent blood of a king, even one who had fallen.
H7394G.origine: The name Recab means "rider" or "one who mounts" in Hebrew, derived from the root that evokes the act of riding. It is a name of function or characteristic that perhaps suggests the military role of the character. The name refers to the image of the horseman, a prestigious figure at the time of the Israelite monarchy.
H7394G.emploi: Recab only appears in the story of the murder of Ish-Bosheth (2 Samuel 4). He is mentioned four times in these few verses: first as one of the two captains in the service of Saul's son, then as one of the two conspirators who carried out the assassination. His role in the narrative is closely linked to that of his brother Baana; the two men always act together and are treated the same way by David, who condemns them with the same severity. This passage shows how Recab, despite his rank as a military chief, committed a political crime that David refused to tolerate.
H7394G.portee: The story of Recab illustrates an important biblical principle: the end does not justify the means. Although the death of Ish-Bosheth might have seemed political and even favorable to David, he refused to condone the murder of a king and punished the assassins. This demonstrates King David's justice and his respect for the order established by God, even towards an adversary. For the reader, this story teaches that faithfulness to God takes precedence over political calculations.

sens: Man living during the divided monarchy, father of Jonadab
Founder of a community dedicated to obedience and abstinence
H7394H.detail:
1. Recab is a historical figure from the Old Testament, father of Jonadab who lived during the time of King Jehu, around the ninth century B.C. He met Jehu and rode with him in his chariot (2 Kings 10:15).
2. Recab is best known as the founder of a strict way of life: he commanded his descendants, the Rechabites, to never drink wine and to live according to principles of absolute obedience. Centuries later, under Jeremiah, his descendants still rigorously adhered to this commitment (Jeremiah 35:6-8), making them models of faithfulness to their word.
H7394H.origine: The name Recab means "rider" or "one who rides a horse," from the Hebrew root evoking chariots or horsemanship. This name likely reflected his function or status in ancient society. Recab was descended from the Kenites, a non-Israelite tribe integrated into the people of Israel (1 Chronicles 2:55). His descendants, the Rechabites, formed a community recognizable by their strict adherence to the rules established by their ancestor.
H7394H.emploi: Recab appears eight times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in 2 Kings and Jeremiah. Under King Jehu, he is a figure of alliance and trust: Jehu seeks him for his integrity and support (2 Kings 10:15-23). The most numerous occurrences are in Jeremiah 35, where the prophet presents the Rechabites as a living example: for over two centuries, Recab's descendants respected their father's prohibition against wine and obedience to his word, better than the Israelites obeyed God (Jeremiah 35:6, 35:8, 35:14). This transgenerational faithfulness makes Recab a rare biblical symbol of successful transmission of a moral requirement.
H7394H.portee: Recab and his descendants teach the Christian reader about the transformative power of obedience and familial faithfulness. The consistency of the Rechabites, who kept their father's command through the centuries without altering it, contrasts with Israel's unfaithfulness to God and invites the believer to meditate on what makes a commitment to God enduring. This story also reminds us that it is not the great heroes, but the obscure faithful, who shape future generations.

sens: Man from the time of the Exile and Return, father of Malchijah
H7394I.detail: 1. Recab is a personal name mentioned only once in the preserved Bible: he is the father of Malchijah, who was chief of the district of Beth-Hakkarem and participated in the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem under Governor Nehemiah (Nehemiah 3:14). His name literally means "one who rides" or "rider," but in this context, it simply refers to a man whose descendants played a role in the restoration work of Jerusalem after the Exile.
H7394I.origine: The name Recab comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the action of riding or mounting (on a horse or pack animal). The word appears in the genealogy of important inhabitants of Jerusalem at the time of the Return from Exile. Ancient tradition also mentioned other Recabs in Israel's history (a father of Jehonadab during King Jehu's time, a captain of Ishbosheth), but in the preserved biblical text, only one is explicitly named.
H7394I.emploi: Recab appears only once in the Bible: in Nehemiah 3:14, where he is identified as the father of Malchijah, chief of the district of Beth-Hakkarem who restored the Dung Gate during the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem after the Exile around 445 B.C. This unique usage places him in an administrative context and public works, among the important men of Jerusalem at the time of Nehemiah.

sens: One who drives a war chariot or a harnessed vehicle
Rider who mounts a horse
Soldier or servant who wields weapons from a chariot
H7395.detail:
1. The charioteer is the person who guides the horses and directs the vehicle in battle. In 1 Kings 22:34, the wounded king of Israel orders his charioteer to turn and take him out of the battlefield — this is a crucial military role, requiring skill and strength.
2. The word can also refer to a rider who mounts a horse, as in 2 Kings 9:17, where the watchman sees a troop approaching and asks to send a rider to meet them to learn the intentions of those who are coming.
3. The charioteer is often an armed warrior, serving kings in critical moments of battle, where it is necessary to master the horses and participate in combat or retreat.
H7395.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of riding or mounting. It is related to the family of the word "chariot" (rakav in Hebrew), which designates the chariot itself. The term encompasses one who rides on the chariot or on the horse, hence its meaning of driver or rider. In biblical Hebrew, this vocabulary belongs to the world of war and royal power.
H7395.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in accounts of battle or military communication. In 1 Kings 22:34 and its parallel in 2 Chronicles 18:33, it designates the charioteer of the king, who obeys the orders of the wounded sovereign. In 2 Kings 9:17, it takes on the nuance of a messenger rider, sent for reconnaissance. The three usages emphasize the strategic and military role: directing, transporting, communicating. It is a figure from the ancient Near Eastern kingdoms, where the chariot was the weapon of prestige and power.
H7395.portee: For the biblical reader, this word reminds us that military and royal power relied on the obedience and dedication of men trained for battle. The charioteer symbolizes the faithful servant who supports the king in the heart of danger. It also provides a window into ancient life: the Bible speaks the language of its time and its weapons, rooting divine revelation in the concrete history of peoples.

sens: action of riding a horse, of mounting
covers or pads used as a saddle or mount
H7396.detail: 1. The word designates the very action of mounting and riding a horse. It is the physical act of moving in this way, practiced by warriors, messengers, and prominent figures in the ancient Near East. 2. By extension, it refers to the equipment used for this action, notably richly decorated coverings that serve as saddles or saddle pads. In Ezekiel 27:20, Dedan trades with Tyre by providing these "covers for sitting on a horse," meaning luxurious saddles or coverings intended to adorn and equip the mounts of important figures.
H7396.origine: The word comes from the root "ركب" (rakab), which means "to mount" or "to ride." It is a feminine form that expresses the action or state of riding. The root is the same as that of the word designating the rider and evokes the context of travel and transport by equids, which were very important in the cultures of the ancient Levant.
H7396.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 27:20, in a passage describing the goods that different nations traded with the Phoenician city of Tyre. In this commercial context, it specifically refers to rich textile articles serving as mount equipment — highly prized luxury goods and an element of international trade at the time. The context emphasizes that even riding accessories were valuable and exchangeable products.
H7396.portee: This term reminds us of the importance of the horse and horsemanship in the political and commercial life of the biblical Near East. For the reader, it illustrates how everyday objects could be high-value goods, worthy of trade between powers, and how Scripture helps us understand the wealth and prestige of Tyre before its judgment.

sens: Descendant de Rechab, fondateur d'une communauté particulière en Israël
Membre d'une famille ou d'un groupe attaché à des règles de vie strictes, notamment l'abstinence de vin
H7397A.detail:
1. Les Rechabites sont les descendants de Rechab, un ancêtre qui a fondé un groupe distinct au sein du peuple d'Israël. Ils forment une communauté reconnaissable, que la Bible appelle « la maison des Rechabites ».
2. Ce qui caractérise les Rechabites, c'est leur obéissance à des commandements stricts transmis par Jonadab, le fils de Rechab. En Jérémie 35, Dieu demande au prophète de les tester en leur offrant du vin à boire, mais ils refusent car c'est interdit par les ordres de leur père Jonadab — ils observent « tous ses commandements » (Jérémie 35:18). Leur fidélité à ces règles anciennes devient pour Dieu un modèle de l'obéissance que le peuple d'Israël aurait dû lui montrer.
H7397A.origine: Le nom vient de Rechab (hébreu רֵכָב), un homme qui a donné naissance à ce groupe distinct d'Israël. Le mot désigne à la fois l'ancêtre fondateur et tous ceux qui descendent de lui et suivent son enseignement. Les Rechabites incarnent l'idée d'une lignée fidèle à la parole d'un père fondateur.
H7397A.emploi: Les Rechabites apparaissent quatre fois dans la Bible, uniquement en Jérémie 35. Dieu envoie Jérémie les chercher et les invite à boire du vin dans le Temple. Bien que la situation soit une sorte d'épreuve — Dieu teste leur fidélité — les Rechabites refusent unanimement, invoquant l'ordre de Jonadab leur père. Dieu reconnaît alors leur obéissance constante et les bénit, tandis qu'il reproche à Juda sa désobéissance chronique. Ce récit unique met en lumière le contraste : une communauté humaine reste fidèle aux paroles de son chef, tandis que le peuple élu abandonne les commandements de l'Éternel.
H7397A.portee: Les Rechabites rappellent au lecteur que la fidélité à la parole donnée est possible et qu'elle plaît à Dieu. Leur exemple montre aussi que l'obéissance peut prendre des formes surprenantes — refuser le vin semble austère, mais elle devient un témoignage. Enfin, leur histoire souligne que Dieu remarque et bénit ceux qui restent constants, même dans un contexte de décadence générale.

sens: Lieu de Judée mentionné une seule fois dans les généalogies bibliques
H7397B.detail: Reca est un endroit situé en Judée, probablement un village ou une petite agglomération. Le seul passage où ce nom apparaît le décrit comme un lieu associé à une famille de bâtisseurs et d'artisans, les « hommes de Reca » (1 Chroniques 4:12), ce qui suggère qu'il s'agissait d'une communauté de métier ou d'une localité caractérisée par des activités de construction et d'artisanat.
H7397B.origine: Le nom Reca signifie littéralement « la partie la plus lointaine » ou « l'extrémité ». Il désigne vraisemblablement un lieu retiré ou périphérique. Certains chercheurs proposent d'identifier Reca avec le village de Rachiah, situé à environ 8 kilomètres au sud de Jérusalem, dans la région de Judée.
H7397B.emploi: Reca n'est mentionné qu'une seule fois dans la Bible, en 1 Chroniques 4:12, dans une généalogie de la tribu de Juda. Le contexte indique que c'était un lieu connu par ses habitants, appelés « les hommes de Reca », probablement une famille ou une communauté d'artisans et de constructeurs établis à cet endroit. Cette brève mention suggère que Reca était un petit centre d'activité économique ou artisanale dans l'ancienne Judée.

sens: Véhicule à roues tiré par des chevaux ou d'autres animaux
Au sens figuré : monture ou moyen de transport majestueux
H7398.detail:
1. Un char est un véhicule construit sur des roues, généralement tiré par des chevaux et utilisé pour le transport ou la guerre. Dans Psaumes 104:3, le psalmiste parle poétiquement de Dieu qui « prend les nuées pour son char », une image grandiose où les nuages deviennent un véhicule majestueux qui porte le Seigneur à travers le ciel.
2. Au sens figuré et poétique, le char désigne tout ce qui peut servir de monture ou de moyen de locomotion à quelqu'un, en particulier pour exprimer la puissance et la majesté. C'est ainsi que les nuées, ordinairement légères et éphémères, sont transformées en un attelage royal et imposant qui porte Dieu lui-même.
H7398.origine: Le mot hébreu רְכוּב (rekhúv) vient de la racine רכב (rakhabh), qui signifie « monter, chevaucher ». Cette racine exprime l'action de s'asseoir sur quelque chose de mobile — un animal ou un véhicule — pour être porté. Elle est apparentée à d'autres mots hébreux relatifs à la cavalerie et au transport, et elle évoque fondamentalement l'idée de dominer ou de contrôler ce qui vous porte. L'arabe conserve des mots similaires issus de cette même racine sémitique ancienne.
H7398.emploi: Ce mot apparaît une seule fois dans la Bible hébraïque, en Psaumes 104:3. C'est une occurrence poétique et majestueuse : le psalmiste décrit Dieu en des termes empruntés à l'imagerie de la royauté terrestre, pour exprimer sa transcendance et sa domination sur la création. L'emploi de ce terme met l'accent sur la puissance de Dieu, qui chevauche les nuées comme un roi chevaucherait son attelage de bataille ou de parade. Ce langage figuré confère à l'éternel une autorité absolue sur les éléments naturels.
H7398.portee: Cette image du char des nuées invite le croyant à contempler la majesté et l'autorité de Dieu sur le monde entier. Elle le rassure en lui montrant que celui qui guide les nuées et fait souffler le vent est le Seigneur vivant, capable de diriger l'histoire et la nature selon sa volonté. Pour celui qui l'adore, c'est une invitation à reconnaître la suprématie divine et à lui faire confiance face aux éléments et aux incertitudes de la vie.

sens: Ensemble de biens matériels possédés : argent, or, objets
Troupeau, bétail, animaux d'élevage
Stocks de nourriture, réserves, provisions
Richesse accumulée, fortune, patrimoine
H7399.detail:
1. Le mot désigne d'abord tout ce qu'on possède comme bien matériel : Abram emporte avec lui « tous les biens qu'ils possédaient » en partant pour Canaan (Genèse 12:5), c'est-à-dire l'argent, l'or, les objets de valeur qu'il a amassés.
2. Il s'applique régulièrement aux troupeaux et au bétail : quand les richesses d'Abram et de Lot deviennent trop importantes, « la contrée où ils séjournaient ne pouvait plus leur suffire à cause de leurs troupeaux » (Genèse 36:7), car c'étaient là leurs « biens ».
3. Il inclut aussi les réserves d'aliments et les ustensiles : dans le retour d'exil, on demande pour la maison de Dieu « de l'argent, de l'or, des effets, et du bétail » (Esdras 1:4) — le mot hébreu couvre tout ce mobilier précieux.
4. Au sens plus large, le mot renvoie à la richesse globale, au patrimoine : quand des ennemis pillent « toutes les richesses » du palais royal (2 Chroniques 21:17), c'est la totalité des possessions qui est saccagée.
H7399.origine: Le mot hébreu rakhoush vient d'une racine qui évoque l'idée de posséder, d'avoir en sa propriété. C'est un terme générique pour tous les biens mobiliers — tout ce qu'on peut transporter ou rassembler, par opposition à la terre elle-même. Dans l'Ancien Testament, il s'oppose à la notion de possessions immobilières (terres, maisons), même s'il peut englober aussi les animaux qui produisent la richesse.
H7399.emploi: Le mot apparaît 27 fois dans l'Ancien Testament, surtout dans les récits des patriarches (Genèse), dans l'histoire des rois de Juda (Chroniques) et dans les textes de l'exil (Esdras, Daniel). Dans la Genèse, il décrit les possessions d'Abram, de Lot et de Jacob, montrant comment la richesse croît et pose des problèmes pratiques (manque de pâturages, jalousies). Dans les Chroniques, il apparaît dans les contextes de guerre et de pillage : les rois accumulaient des « richesses » et les ennemis venaient les dépouiller. Dans Esdras et Daniel, le mot sert à décrire ce que les conquérants s'appropriaient ou ce qu'on devait donner pour reconstruire le Temple. Le sens reste stable : toujours la possession matérielle, souvent fragile et exposée.
H7399.portee: Ce mot rappelle au lecteur que la richesse matérielle — or, bétail, possessions — est une réalité constante de la vie humaine, mais aussi profondément vulnérable : elle peut être perdue par la guerre, la famine ou le jugement de Dieu. Elle ne fait jamais l'objet d'une condamnation morale directe dans ces textes, mais plutôt d'une constatation réaliste : on possède, on peut perdre. Pour le croyant, cela invite à ne pas mettre sa confiance dans l'accumulation, puisque les « richesses » les mieux gardées peuvent disparaître en un instant.
